lessons.plain: Structured data is information arranged in a fixed, predictable layout: a table of rows and columns, where every row has the same columns and each column holds one kind of value. A spreadsheet of employees is a good picture. Every row is one person, and every column, such as name, start date or salary, means the same thing all the way down. Because the layout is agreed in advance, a computer can sort, filter, total and join this data quickly and reliably. The trade-off is rigidity. Every new piece of information has to fit the agreed shape, or the shape itself has to be changed first.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop keeps its orders in a table with the columns OrderID, CustomerName, OrderDate and Total. Someone tries to add an order that also has a 'gift message', but there is no column for it. What do you think happens, and what would the shop have to do to store that message?
lessons.teach:
Structured data is data that follows a schema. A schema is a design, decided before any data is stored, that says which fields exist and what type of value each field may hold. The data lives in a table, which is a grid of rows and columns. A row (also called a record) is one item, such as one order. A column (also called a field or attribute) is one property, such as the order date. A data type is the kind of value a column accepts, such as whole number, decimal, text or date. Most tables also have a primary key, which is a column whose value uniquely identifies each row, such as OrderID. A relational database is a system that stores many such tables and links them through shared key values.

This works because everything is predictable. The system knows every row's shape, so it can check new data on the way in, build fast lookups and answer questions like 'total sales in March' without guessing what each row contains.

Here is a worked example. Take an Orders table with OrderID (whole number, primary key), OrderDate (date) and Total (decimal). First, inserting 1001, 2024-03-02, 49.90 succeeds because it matches the schema. Second, inserting 1002, 'next Tuesday', 20.00 is rejected, because 'next Tuesday' is not a valid date. Third, inserting another row with OrderID 1001 is rejected, because the primary key must be unique. Finally, adding a gift message needs a schema change: a new GiftMessage column added to the table. Every existing row then gets an empty value for it.

A common mistake is to assume data is structured just because it sits in a database or a file. What makes data structured is the fixed schema, not where it is stored. A CSV file with consistent columns is structured.

In a running system, the schema protects data quality. The cost is that when requirements change, the schema must be changed first, and on large tables that change can take a long time.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic keeps an Appointments table with this schema: ApptID (whole number, primary key), ApptDate (date) and DurationMinutes (whole number). Trace these inserts. Step 1: inserting 7301, 2025-06-10, 30 succeeds because every value matches its column's data type. Step 2: inserting 7302, 2025-06-11, 'forty-five' is ____. Step 3: inserting another row with ApptID 7301 is rejected because the primary key must be unique. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: rejected, because 'forty-five' is text and DurationMinutes only accepts whole numbers
accepted, because the value is stored as text and checked later in a report
rejected, because ApptID 7302 already identifies another row in the table
accepted, because the system converts the words into the number 45 automatically
questions.why: The schema fixes DurationMinutes as a whole number, so the system checks the value on the way in and rejects text that is not a valid whole number.

questions.prompt: A colleague says: "Our customer notes are stored inside a database, so they must be structured data." According to the definition of structured data, what actually makes data structured?
choices: It is stored in a database server rather than in files
It follows a fixed schema that sets the fields and each field's data type
It is small enough to fit in a single file
It has been cleaned by a data engineer before use
questions.why: Structured data is defined by a fixed schema decided in advance, not by where the data is stored.

questions.prompt: A bus company exports trip logs to a CSV file. Every line has the same four columns in the same order: TripID, RouteNumber, DepartureTime and PassengerCount, and each column always holds the same kind of value. How should this data be classified?
choices: Not structured, because it is a file rather than a database table
Structured, because every record follows the same consistent columns and value types
Structured only after it is loaded into a relational database
Not structured, because a CSV file cannot have a primary key column
questions.why: A file with consistent columns and value types follows a fixed schema, which is what makes data structured.

questions.prompt: An online shop has a Products table with 50 million rows. The business now wants to record a CountryOfOrigin for each product. What happens in a structured-data system?
choices: New rows can include CountryOfOrigin right away with no change to the table
A new CountryOfOrigin column must be added first; existing rows get an empty value, and on a table this large the change may take a long time
The database guesses a country for each existing row from the product name
The existing rows are deleted and must be re-inserted with the new value
questions.why: In structured data the schema must change before new kinds of values can be stored; existing rows get an empty value for the new column, and changes on large tables can be slow.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why the customer list is called 'structured data' while the support emails are not. Explain in your own words what makes data structured, and name one limit or trade-off of storing data this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: Structured data follows a schema, which is a layout agreed in advance. It is stored in tables: each row is one item, like one customer, and each column is one property, like email or signup date. Every row has the same columns, and each column holds one data type, so a date column only accepts dates. Usually a primary key, such as CustomerID, uniquely identifies each row. Because the shape is fixed, the database can reject bad values, search quickly and total or join tables reliably. The support emails have no fixed set of fields, so they are not structured in this sense. The trade-off is rigidity. If we suddenly want to record something new, like a preferred language, we have to change the schema first and add a column for every row. On big tables that is slow, and it has to be planned.
rubricPoints: States that structured data follows a schema defined before data is stored.
Describes tables of rows and columns where every row has the same columns.
Mentions that each column has a data type and that a key can uniquely identify rows.
Explains that the fixed shape enables validation and fast, reliable querying.
Names rigidity as a limit: new kinds of information require a schema change first.

suggested.rationale: A SQL lab would let the learner define a table schema, watch rows that break the data types or the primary key get rejected, and add a column, which makes the features of structured data concrete.

lessons.plain: Semi-structured data is information that carries its own labels but does not follow one fixed layout. Each record says what its pieces are, like "name" or "phone", yet different records may have different pieces, and pieces can sit inside other pieces. Think of a stack of index cards where everyone wrote labeled notes. Every card says "Name:" before the name, but one card also lists three pets and another lists none. You can still find things because of the labels, even though no two cards have to match exactly.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two online shoppers sign up. One gives a name and email. The other gives a name, email, and two delivery addresses. If both are saved as labeled records without forcing them into the same columns, is that data organized, disorganized, or somewhere in between? Why?
lessons.teach:
Semi-structured data is data whose structure travels with the data itself rather than being fixed in advance. A schema is the agreed shape of the data: which fields exist and what type each holds. Structured data, like a database table, has a rigid schema that every row must match. Unstructured data, like a photo, has no fields at all. Semi-structured data sits between them. Each record is self-describing, meaning it carries field names (also called keys or tags) next to its values. Records in the same collection may have different fields, and fields can be nested, meaning a field holds a group of other fields or a list. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation, a text format of key-value pairs in braces) is the most common example.

This works because a reader does not need a separate rulebook to interpret a record. It reads the labels. That makes it easy to store data whose shape varies or changes over time.

Worked example. Record A: {"name": "Ana", "email": "ana@x.com"}. Record B: {"name": "Raj", "email": "raj@x.com", "addresses": [{"city": "Leeds"}, {"city": "York"}]}. Step 1: both records have labels, so the data is not unstructured. Step 2: B has a field A lacks, so there is no single fixed column layout. Step 3: B's addresses field holds a list of nested records, which is a hierarchy that a flat table would struggle with. Conclusion: semi-structured.

A common mistake is to think semi-structured means messy or unreliable. It is organized. It is just flexible per record. A related error is assuming every record has every field. In a running system, code that reads record["addresses"] without checking will crash or return errors on records like Ana's, so readers must handle missing or extra fields.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery startup stores each order as a JSON record. Order 1041: {"item": "pizza", "qty": 2}. Order 1042: {"item": "salad", "qty": 1, "extras": {"dressing": "lemon", "croutons": false}}. An analyst is writing report code that reads every order's dressing choice. Step 1: every value sits next to a key such as "item" or "qty", so each record is self-describing and can be read without a separate rulebook. Step 2: ______. Step 3: so the report code must first check whether an order has an "extras" field before reading its dressing, or it will fail on orders like 1041. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: The records have no fixed columns, so the data has no labels and is really unstructured.
Order 1041 lacks the "extras" field that 1042 has, so records do not all share the same fields.
Both orders must match one table schema, so "extras" is guaranteed to exist in every order.
Varying fields mean the data is messy and unreliable, so order 1041 should be deleted.
questions.why: Records in a semi-structured collection can have different fields, and that missing "extras" field in order 1041 is exactly why the code in Step 3 must check before reading it.

questions.prompt: A logistics company describes its shipment records as "self-describing." What does that term mean for semi-structured data?
choices: Every record is guaranteed to have exactly the same columns in the same order.
The shape of every record is defined once, in a separate schema document stored elsewhere.
Each record carries its field names (keys) right next to its values, so a reader can interpret it from the labels.
The records contain no fields at all, like an image or an audio clip.
questions.why: Self-describing means the labels travel with the data inside each record, so no separate rulebook is needed to read it.

questions.prompt: A city museum keeps three datasets: scanned photographs of its paintings; a ticket-sales table where every row has the same columns (date, price, gate); and exhibit descriptions stored as JSON, where some exhibits include a nested "loanedFrom" field holding a lender's name and country while others omit it. Which dataset is semi-structured?
choices: All three, because any stored data has some organisation.
The ticket-sales table, because it contains both numbers and dates.
The scanned photographs, because each image file has a name and a size.
The JSON exhibit descriptions, because records are labelled, can differ in fields, and can nest.
questions.why: The exhibit descriptions are labelled key-value records whose fields vary and can nest, while the photos have no fields and the table follows one rigid schema.

questions.prompt: A fitness app stores each workout as a JSON record. Running workouts include a "heartRate" field, but swimming workouts were saved without one. A developer's summary code reads record["heartRate"] on every workout without checking. What is the most likely result in the running system?
choices: JSON automatically fills in a heartRate of 0 for any record that lacks it.
The swimming records count as unstructured data, so the code skips them safely.
The storage system rejects any workout missing heartRate, so this cannot happen.
The code crashes or returns errors on swimming workouts, so it must handle missing fields.
questions.why: Semi-structured records do not all have every field, so code that assumes a field exists will fail on records that lack it unless it checks first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what makes data semi-structured, how it differs from a table and from a photo, and name one tradeoff of its flexibility.
lessons.modelAnswer: Semi-structured data is labeled but not locked into one fixed shape. Each record carries its own field names next to the values, so it describes itself. A JSON document is the usual example. Unlike a database table, records don't all need the same fields. One customer can have a phone number and another can skip it. Fields can also nest lists or sub-records, like several addresses inside one customer. Unlike a photo or free text, there are clear labels, so you can still find specific values. The flexibility is useful when the shape varies or changes, because you don't redesign a table every time. The tradeoff is that nothing guarantees a field exists or has the right type. Any code or query reading the data has to check for missing or unexpected fields. A fixed schema would catch those problems up front.
rubricPoints: States that each record carries its own field names, so it is self-describing.
Notes that records in one collection can have different fields with no single fixed schema.
Mentions nesting or hierarchy, such as lists or sub-records inside a field.
Distinguishes it from structured tables and from unstructured content like images.
Names a tradeoff, such as readers having to handle missing or inconsistent fields.

suggested.rationale: Turning flat CSV rows into JSON makes the learner build labeled, nestable records by hand, which shows how semi-structured data differs from a fixed table.

lessons.plain: Unstructured data is information that does not come arranged in fields, rows or labeled parts that a computer can read directly. Photos, videos, audio recordings, scanned documents, emails and free-form text are common examples. Think of a shoebox full of letters and holiday photos: everything valuable is in there, but nothing is sorted into labeled folders, so to answer a question like 'which letters mention a refund?' you have to open and read each one. Unstructured data is often the largest share of what organizations store, and getting value from it usually takes extra processing.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company keeps thousands of recorded customer phone calls. Could you ask a computer 'how many callers were angry last week?' as easily as you could ask 'how many calls happened last week?' Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Unstructured data is data with no predefined data model, meaning there is no agreed set of named fields, types or relationships that describes its content. Images, video, audio, PDFs, scanned forms, chat messages and long free text all fall here.

Why this matters: a computer can only filter, sort or total what it can find in a predictable place. A structured table puts a price in the 'price' column every time. In a photo or a recording, the meaning (a face, a complaint, a signature) is buried inside the content itself, so you cannot query it directly. To use it, you first store it, usually as whole files or objects in a file or object store (a service that keeps files of any type, each with a name and some descriptive tags called metadata), and then extract meaning with processing such as optical character recognition (turning images of text into text), speech-to-text, or AI image analysis.

Worked example: a help desk receives a ticket. Step 1, look at the ticket number, date and customer ID: these sit in fixed fields, so they are not unstructured. Step 2, look at the attached screenshot: it is pixels with no fields describing what it shows, so it is unstructured. Step 3, look at the voice-message attachment: also unstructured. Step 4, ask 'can I search for tickets where the screenshot shows an error code?' Not until something reads the image and writes the code into a field.

Common mistake: thinking unstructured means 'no format at all'. A JPEG or MP3 file has a precise file format; what is missing is a model describing the content's meaning. Likewise, a block of free text stored in a database column is still unstructured content.

In a running system, unstructured data tends to be large and fast-growing, so storage cost, retention rules and the processing pipeline needed to make it searchable become real design concerns.

questions.prompt: A car insurer reviews one claim record to decide which parts are unstructured. Step 1: the policy number, claim date and claimed amount (2,400) sit in fixed, named fields, so they are not unstructured. Step 2: the four photos of the dented bumper are pixels with no fields describing what they show, so they are unstructured. Step 3: the scanned handwritten witness statement is an image of a page with no fields describing its meaning, so it is also unstructured. Step 4: an analyst asks, 'Can I list every claim where the witness statement mentions a second vehicle?' What is the correct answer for Step 4?
choices: Yes, because the statement is saved in the same claim record as the policy number and date.
Never, because unstructured data cannot be used for any kind of search or analysis.
Yes, because a scanned PDF has a precise file format that the system can query directly.
Not until processing such as optical character recognition reads the scan and writes the relevant text into a searchable field.
questions.why: The meaning is buried inside the image, so it can only be searched after processing such as OCR extracts it into a predictable field.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes what makes data unstructured?
choices: Its files have no file format, so software cannot open them.
It is always stored in a file or object store rather than a database.
It is too large to fit in a single table.
It has no predefined data model, meaning no agreed set of named fields, types or relationships describing its content.
questions.why: Unstructured data is defined by the absence of a model describing the content's meaning, not by missing formats, location or size.

questions.prompt: A land-survey company captures about 8,000 aerial drone video clips every month and wants to find clips showing flooded roads. Which set of concerns is most important when designing for this data in a running system?
choices: None, because video files already have a precise format and are searchable as stored.
Storage cost, retention rules, and a processing pipeline, such as AI image analysis, to make the content searchable.
Adding relationships between clips so the database can total the flooded roads directly.
Choosing a fixed column type for each video so the clips can be sorted by content.
questions.why: Unstructured data tends to be large and fast-growing, and its meaning must be extracted by processing before it can be searched.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop stores customer reviews in a relational table. Each row has a numeric rating from 1 to 5 in one column and the reviewer's free-text comments in a 'review_text' column. How should the content of 'review_text' be classified?
choices: Unstructured content, because free text has no model describing its meaning, even when stored in a database column.
Structured, because it sits in a named column of a table.
Structured, because the column has a defined text data type.
Not data at all until a person reads and summarises it.
questions.why: Placing free text in a database column gives it a location, but its meaning still has no predefined model, so it remains unstructured content.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says 'everything we save is just data, so we can query the call recordings the same way we query the orders table.' Explain to them in your own words what makes the recordings unstructured, and name the tradeoff or limit that comes with keeping data in this form.
lessons.modelAnswer: The orders table has a data model: every row has the same named fields, like order ID, date and amount, so a query knows exactly where to look. The call recordings don't. Each one is an audio file, and while the file format itself is well defined, the meaning inside, such as what the customer asked for or whether they were upset, isn't stored in any labeled field. That is what makes it unstructured. We can easily store the recordings as files with some metadata, like call date and agent, and we can query that metadata. But to ask about the content we first need a processing step, such as speech-to-text and then analysis, to pull facts out into fields. The tradeoff is that unstructured data is flexible and captures rich detail, but it is large, costly to keep, and not directly searchable without that extra work.
rubricPoints: Defines unstructured data as having no predefined data model or named fields describing its content.
Gives correct examples such as images, audio, video, documents or free text.
Distinguishes a file format from a data model, noting that a well-defined file can still hold unstructured content.
Explains that the content cannot be queried directly and needs processing to extract meaning.
Notes that metadata about the file can be queried even when the content cannot.
Names a tradeoff such as large storage size and cost or the extra processing effort.

suggested.rationale: The unit's core skill is classifying described datasets, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that mix fixed fields with attachments and media builds that judgment best.

lessons.plain: A data file format is the agreed layout used to write data into a file so that another program can read it back correctly. Think of it like choosing between a spreadsheet, a letter, or a sealed parcel. Each one packs the same information in a different way. Some formats are plain text that a person can open and read, such as comma-separated lists or labelled text. Others are compact binary layouts built for computers, used for images, or for analysing huge tables quickly. Picking the right format affects how easy the data is to share, how big the file is, and how fast it can be queried.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a list of 10 million vehicle trips and analysts usually ask for just two of its thirty columns. Would you rather store it in a file that keeps each trip together on one line, or one that keeps each column's values together? Why?
lessons.teach:
A data file format is the rule for how values are laid out inside a file. The common ones fall into three groups.

Text formats are human-readable. Delimited text separates values with a chosen character, the delimiter. The best-known is CSV (comma-separated values): one record per line, fields split by commas, often with a header row naming the columns. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) stores data as key-value pairs inside curly braces, and it can nest objects and lists, so records need not share identical fields. XML (Extensible Markup Language) wraps each value in named opening and closing tags. It is wordier than JSON and mostly seen in older systems.

Binary formats store raw bytes that only software interprets. A BLOB (binary large object) is any such file, for example an image, video or PDF.

Optimized formats are binary formats designed for big data. Avro is row-based, meaning each record is stored together, and it carries its own schema (a description of the fields). That makes it good for streaming and writing records one at a time. ORC (Optimized Row Columnar) and Parquet are columnar, meaning all values of one column are stored together. A query reading two columns skips the rest, and similar values compress well, so analytics run faster and cost less storage.

Worked example: one vehicle reading. In CSV, the header is id,speed,city and the record is 42,61,Leeds. In JSON it becomes {"id":42,"speed":61,"city":"Leeds"}. Each JSON value carries its own label, so it is larger but self-describing. Stored in Parquet across a million rows, the speed values sit side by side. An average-speed query reads only that column.

A common mistake is forgetting that a comma can appear inside a value, such as a city named Leeds, UK. Unless that field is wrapped in quotes, the parser sees an extra column. Every later field then shifts, and loads fail or, worse, silently store wrong data.

questions.prompt:
A bakery chain exports its daily sales as a CSV file. Trace what happens when one product name contains a comma.
Step 1: The header row is product,price,qty, so the parser expects three fields per record.
Step 2: One record is written without quotes as: Bread, seeded,2.40,15
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The fix is to wrap that field in quotes, "Bread, seeded", so the parser treats it as one value.
Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The parser notices the missing quotes and skips that one record, so the rest of the file loads normally.
The parser splits at every comma, finds four fields instead of three, and the values shift: " seeded" lands in the price column and 2.40 lands in qty.
The parser reads the first comma-separated piece as the product and ignores anything after the third comma, so only the name is shortened.
The parser treats the comma as part of the text because the word "seeded" is not a number, so the record loads correctly.
questions.why: A CSV parser splits at every comma it sees outside quotes, so an unquoted comma inside a value creates an extra field and shifts every later value into the wrong column.

questions.prompt: A ride-sharing app sends trip events to a data platform one record at a time as each trip ends. The team wants a compact binary format that keeps each record together and carries its own schema, meaning a description of its fields. Which format fits best?
choices: Parquet
CSV
XML
Avro
questions.why: Avro is a row-based binary format that stores each record together and embeds its schema, which suits streaming and writing records one at a time.

questions.prompt: A gym stores member profiles. Some members have no emergency contact, some have one, and some list several phone numbers, each with its own label. The team wants a human-readable text format where records do not all need identical fields and values can be nested lists. Which format suits this best?
choices: ORC, because it compresses similar values well
JSON, because it uses key-value pairs that can nest objects and lists
Delimited text such as CSV, because each line is one record
A BLOB, because it can hold any kind of content
questions.why: JSON can nest objects and lists, and records need not share identical fields, which suits profiles with varying contact details.

questions.prompt: An energy company keeps 2 billion rows of smart-meter data with 40 columns. Analysts usually run queries that read only 2 of those columns, such as meter ID and kilowatt-hours. Why would Parquet suit this better than CSV?
choices: Parquet is columnar, so a query reads only the needed columns, and similar values stored together compress well
Parquet is human-readable, so analysts can inspect the file directly
Parquet wraps each value in named tags, which makes every value self-describing
Parquet stores each full record together, so whole rows are read faster
questions.why: Columnar formats such as Parquet store all values of one column together, so a query can skip unneeded columns, and similar values compress well, which lowers both query time and storage cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the main families of data file formats, when you would pick CSV or JSON versus Parquet, and one tradeoff you accept with each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: File formats are just agreed layouts for data on disk. Text formats like CSV, JSON and XML are readable by people and almost any tool. CSV is a simple delimited table with one record per line. JSON uses labelled key-value pairs and can nest, so it suits records whose fields vary. XML does similar work with tags but is wordier. Binary files, often called BLOBs, hold things like images. For big analytics we use optimized binary formats. Avro is row-based with an embedded schema, which is good for writing streams of records. Parquet and ORC are columnar, so queries read only the columns they need and data compresses well. The tradeoff is that text formats are easy to inspect and share but are large and slow to scan at scale. CSV can also break on unquoted delimiters. Columnar formats are fast and compact but you cannot read them by eye and need tooling.
rubricPoints: Defines a file format as the layout used to store data in a file.
Names delimited text/CSV, JSON and XML as human-readable text formats.
Identifies BLOBs as binary files such as images or video.
Distinguishes row-based Avro from columnar Parquet and ORC.
States that columnar formats speed up analytical queries and compress well.
Names a tradeoff such as readability versus size and speed, or delimiter problems in CSV.

suggested.rationale: Converting a real CSV file into JSON makes the learner handle header rows, delimiters and key-value structure directly.

lessons.plain: A data store is any place a system keeps data so it can be found and used again later. Some stores are simple: files sitting in folders or a big storage bucket. Others are databases, which are programs built to organize data and answer questions about it quickly. Think of a household. A shoebox of photos is a file store: cheap, holds anything, but finding one picture means digging. A filing cabinet with labelled folders is a database: you agree on a layout up front, and in return you can find, change and cross-reference things fast.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop must store product photos, customer orders, and a 'customers who bought this also bought' map of links between products. Would you put all three in the same kind of store? Make a guess for each.
lessons.teach:
A data store is a system that keeps data durably so it can be read later. There are two broad families. File stores hold whole files (documents, images, CSV exports) in folders or in object storage, a cheap service that keeps any file as a blob with a name. They take any content but understand nothing inside it, so you read the whole file to search it.

A database is software that organizes data and lets you query it, meaning ask targeted questions and get just the matching items. A relational database keeps data in tables: rows are records, columns are fields, and a schema (the agreed list of columns and types) is enforced on every write. Tables link through keys, and you query them with SQL, the standard query language for relational data. Strict structure is what makes joins and reliable updates possible.

Non-relational databases (often called NoSQL) relax that structure. A key-value store looks up a value by a unique key, very fast but only by that key. A document database stores self-describing records, usually JSON, and each one may have different fields. A column-family database groups related columns so huge, sparse datasets read efficiently. A graph database stores nodes (things) and edges (relationships) so that following connections is cheap.

Worked example, the shop from the question. Product photos are large files that are never searched by their content, so they go to file or object storage. Orders have fixed fields and link to customers and products, and totals must be correct, so a relational database fits. The 'also bought' links are relationships you follow hop by hop, so a graph database fits best.

A common mistake is assuming NoSQL means 'no structure, so always more flexible and better.' Flexibility moves the checking into your application. In a running system, a missing field that a relational schema would have rejected slips into a document store and breaks reports weeks later. Pick the store by how the data is shaped and how it will be queried.

questions.prompt: A regional library network is choosing where to keep three kinds of data. Step 1: Scanned images of historic maps, each around 200 MB, are stored and displayed but never searched by what is inside the image, so they go to file or object storage. Step 2: Loan records have the same fixed fields every time (member ID, book ID, due date, fine owed), link to member and book tables, and fines must always add up correctly, so a relational database fits. Step 3: The website keeps a small blob of session data for each logged-in visitor, and the app only ever fetches it by the visitor's session ID, millions of times a day, with no other kind of search. Which store fits Step 3, and why?
choices: A relational database, because session data should have an enforced schema like the loans
Object storage, because session data is a small file that needs no structure at all
A key-value store, because every read is a fast lookup by one unique key, the session ID
A graph database, because each session connects a visitor to the books they view
questions.why: The session data is only ever retrieved by a single unique key at high speed, which is exactly what a key-value store does well.

questions.prompt: A smart-thermostat maker collects readings as JSON records. Older models send temperature and humidity; newer models also send air quality and occupancy, and next year's models will add fields nobody has defined yet. The team wants to store each reading as a self-describing record and query by its fields. Which type of data store fits best?
choices: A graph database, because the devices are connected to one another
A document database, because each JSON record can carry different fields
A file store, because JSON readings are just text files in folders
A relational database, because every reading must match one fixed schema
questions.why: A document database stores self-describing JSON records where each one may have different fields, matching readings whose fields vary by model.

questions.prompt: A travel agency moved its customer profiles from a relational database to a document database because it was 'more flexible.' Two months later, the monthly revenue-by-country report started failing because some profiles had no country field at all. What best explains this?
choices: The report must be written in SQL, which document databases can never run
Without an enforced schema, nothing rejected the missing field, so the checking the schema used to do now falls to the application
Document databases cannot store text fields such as country names reliably
Object storage was needed instead, since customer profiles are really files
questions.why: A relational schema would have rejected a write missing the field; a flexible document store accepts it, so the gap only surfaces later when reports run.

questions.prompt: An events company stores ticket bookings in a key-value store, using the booking number as the key. A manager now asks for a list of every booking with a ticket price over 150. What is the core problem?
choices: A key-value store finds values quickly only by their key, so searching by price inside the values is not what it is built for
Key-value stores enforce a strict schema, so the price column cannot be added
Booking numbers are relationships, so the data should have been in a graph database
A key-value store cannot hold numbers, so ticket prices were never saved
questions.why: Key-value lookups are very fast but only by the unique key, so a query on a field inside the value, like price, does not fit the store.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a file store, a relational database and the main kinds of non-relational database, and name one tradeoff you accept when you choose a flexible non-relational store over a relational one.
lessons.modelAnswer: A file store just keeps whole files, like images or CSV exports, in folders or object storage. It is cheap and takes anything, but it does not understand what is inside, so searching means reading files. A database organizes data so you can query it. A relational database uses tables with a fixed schema, links tables with keys, and is queried with SQL, which suits records like orders that must stay consistent. Non-relational stores relax that: key-value stores fetch a value by key very fast, document stores hold JSON records that can differ, column-family stores handle huge sparse data, and graph stores make following relationships cheap. The tradeoff is that with a flexible store the database no longer enforces structure, so bad or missing fields can get in unless the application checks them, and cross-record joins are harder.
rubricPoints: Defines a data store and separates file stores from databases.
States that relational databases use tables, an enforced schema, keys and SQL.
Names key-value, document, column-family and graph stores with what each is good at.
Ties the choice of store to the data's shape and how it will be queried.
Names a tradeoff such as weaker enforced structure or harder joins in non-relational stores.

suggested.rationale: This objective is tested by reading a short workload description and picking the right kind of store, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Picking an Azure datastore means matching the shape of your data and how it will be used to the storage service built for that job. Think of a kitchen: you would not keep soup in a spice rack or flour in the fridge door. Neatly organised rows with strict rules go in a relational database, flexible records that change shape go in a document database, and big files like photos or videos go in object storage. Azure offers a managed service for each kind, so the main skill is reading a short description of a workload and naming which container fits.
lessons.guessPrompt: A photo-sharing app needs to keep millions of uploaded pictures. Would you store them as rows in a strict table of columns, or as files in a large storage bucket? Why?
lessons.teach:
Identifying a datastore means reading a use case and choosing the Azure service whose design fits the data's shape and access pattern. Three questions do most of the work: Is the data structured (fixed columns), semi-structured (records like JSON documents whose fields can vary), or unstructured (files such as images, video, PDFs)? Is the workload transactional (many small reads and writes that must stay consistent) or analytical (big scans to answer questions)? And does it need files, rows, or documents?

The main matches are these. Azure SQL Database, Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Azure Database for MySQL are managed relational databases: tables with enforced columns, relationships between tables, and transactions, meaning a group of changes that all succeed or all fail. Azure Cosmos DB is a managed NoSQL (non-relational) database for semi-structured documents or key-value pairs that can be copied across regions for fast reads worldwide. Azure Blob Storage is object storage: a cheap, huge store for unstructured files. Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 is Blob Storage with a folder hierarchy, tuned for analytics over large file sets. Azure Files provides network file shares that servers can mount like a drive. An analytical store such as a data warehouse holds cleaned history for reporting.

Worked example, an online shop. Step one: orders and payments have fixed fields and must never half-save, so they are structured and transactional; choose Azure SQL Database. Step two: product photos are unstructured files; choose Blob Storage. Step three: customer profiles where each person stores different preferences are semi-structured JSON needing quick reads in many countries; choose Cosmos DB. Step four: years of sales history for trend reports is analytical; land it in Data Lake Storage and a warehouse.

A common mistake is forcing everything into one relational database, including images and changing-shape records. In a running system this bloats the database, slows backups and queries, and raises cost, while the opposite mistake, using a document store for heavily related, join-heavy data, makes consistency hard to keep.

questions.prompt: A city library network is choosing datastores. Step one: loan records (book ID, member ID, loan date, due date) have fixed fields and a checkout must never half-save, so the data is structured and transactional; choose Azure SQL Database. Step two: the library is scanning 40,000 rare manuscripts into high-resolution image files. Which store fits? (This is the missing step.) Step three: member reading-preference profiles, where each member saves different settings as JSON and the library app is read in several countries, are semi-structured; choose Azure Cosmos DB. Step four: twelve years of loan history for trend reports is analytical; land it in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 and a data warehouse.
choices: Azure SQL Database, storing each image in a table column next to the loan records
Azure Blob Storage, because the scans are unstructured files that need cheap, large-scale object storage
A data warehouse, because 40,000 large images is a big volume of data
Azure Cosmos DB, because files that are not in table form should go in a NoSQL database
questions.why: Scanned images are unstructured files, and Blob Storage is the cheap, very large object store built for files like these.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2?
choices: A network file share that servers mount like a drive
Blob Storage with a folder hierarchy, tuned for analytics over large sets of files
A managed relational database that enforces columns and transactions
A NoSQL document database that copies data across regions for fast reads
questions.why: Data Lake Storage Gen2 is Blob-style object storage plus a folder hierarchy, designed for analytical work over many files.

questions.prompt: A factory runs six older application servers that all need to read and write the same set of configuration files through a shared drive letter, the way they did on the old office network. Which Azure store fits?
choices: Azure Blob Storage
Azure Database for MySQL
Azure Cosmos DB
Azure Files
questions.why: Azure Files provides network file shares that servers can mount like a drive, which matches this need for a shared drive.

questions.prompt: A delivery company stores every driver's dashcam video directly inside its Azure SQL Database, alongside its delivery and billing tables. What is the most likely effect on the running system?
choices: The database bloats, so backups and queries slow down and costs rise
The videos are automatically moved into Blob Storage at no cost
The database stops supporting transactions for the billing tables
The videos lose quality because relational tables compress them
questions.why: Forcing unstructured files into a relational database bloats it, which slows backups and queries and raises cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between Azure SQL Database, Azure Cosmos DB and Azure Blob Storage for a new feature, and name one tradeoff of choosing a non-relational store.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the shape of the data and how it is used. If it has fixed columns, relationships between tables, and changes that must all succeed or all fail, like orders or bank transfers, I pick a relational store such as Azure SQL Database. If the records are JSON documents whose fields vary from item to item and we need fast reads or writes at large scale, possibly in several regions, I pick Azure Cosmos DB. If the data is whole files like images, videos or backups, I pick Blob Storage, or Data Lake Storage Gen2 if we will run analytics over those files. The tradeoff with Cosmos DB is flexibility versus structure: we gain schema freedom and global scale, but lose easy joins across entities and the database no longer enforces relationships for us, so the application has to keep related data consistent.
rubricPoints: Classifies data as structured, semi-structured or unstructured before choosing.
Maps structured transactional data to a relational service such as Azure SQL Database.
Maps flexible JSON or key-value records needing scale to Azure Cosmos DB.
Maps unstructured files to Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage Gen2.
Names a real tradeoff, such as losing joins and enforced relationships in a NoSQL store.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by giving short workload descriptions to match to a service, so reasoning through several mixed scenarios builds the skill best and no existing mission covers Azure datastore choice.

lessons.plain: A transactional workload is the everyday record-keeping a business does as things happen: a sale at a till, a bank transfer, a seat booked on a flight. Each piece of work is small and quick, touches only a few records, and many people do this work at once. The system has to get every one exactly right, every time. Think of a careful shop clerk with a ledger. Each customer's purchase is written down completely or not at all. Two clerks can never sell the same last item. Once it is in the ledger, it stays there even if the lights go out.
lessons.guessPrompt: You move 100 dollars from your savings to your checking account, and the system crashes halfway through. What should the bank's system make sure has happened to your money once it comes back up?
lessons.teach:
A transactional workload, often called OLTP (online transaction processing), is a system that records business events as they happen, using many small, fast reads and writes made by many users at the same time. Typical examples are orders, payments, bookings and stock updates. A transaction is a group of changes that the database treats as one unit of work. It finishes with a commit, which makes the changes permanent, or a rollback, which undoes them.

Transactional systems are trusted because they follow ACID, a set of four guarantees. Atomicity means all of a transaction's changes happen, or none of them do. Consistency means a transaction moves the data from one valid state to another and never breaks the rules the database enforces, such as "a balance cannot go below zero." Isolation means transactions running at the same time do not see each other's half-finished work. Durability means a committed change survives a crash or power loss. The data is usually stored normalized, meaning it is split into related tables so each fact is stored once. That keeps writes small and avoids conflicting copies of the same fact.

Worked example: you transfer 100 from savings to checking. Step 1: the transaction begins. Step 2: savings is reduced by 100. Step 3: the server crashes before checking is increased. Step 4: on restart, the database sees the transaction never committed and rolls it back, so savings returns to its original balance. Because of atomicity, no money vanishes. If the crash had come after the commit, durability would guarantee that both changes were kept.

A common mistake is to call any system that holds business data "transactional." A system that scans years of sales history to produce trends is an analytical workload, even if it holds the same data. Transactional work is small, current and write-heavy. Without these guarantees, a running system could double-sell the last concert seat or lose a payment halfway through.

questions.prompt: A hardware wholesaler's database enforces the rule "stock on hand cannot go below zero." A trade customer orders 8 boxes of hinges, but only 5 boxes are in stock. Step 1: a transaction begins. Step 2: a new order line for 8 boxes is written. Step 3: the transaction tries to reduce stock from 5 to -3, which breaks the database's rule. Step 4: ? What should happen in Step 4 for the system to keep its ACID guarantees?
choices: The stock is set to zero instead of -3, and the transaction commits with the 8-box order line.
The transaction commits with stock at -3, and a later report flags the negative value for staff to fix.
The order line is kept and committed, and only the stock change is skipped so the rule is not broken.
The database rejects the change and rolls back the whole transaction, so the order line is undone too.
questions.why: Consistency stops the rule from being broken and atomicity means none of the transaction's changes are kept, so the order line must be rolled back along with the failed stock update.

questions.prompt: A chain of gyms has two systems. System A records each member check-in at the front desk as it happens, across 40 sites at once. System B reads three years of check-ins every Sunday to chart which hours are busiest. Which statement is correct?
choices: System B is the transactional workload, because it processes far more rows at a time.
Neither is transactional, because check-ins involve no payments or money.
Both are transactional workloads, because both hold the same check-in records.
System A is a transactional (OLTP) workload; System B is an analytical workload.
questions.why: System A makes many small, current writes by many users at once, which is OLTP, while System B scans long history to find trends, which is analytical work even though the data is the same.

questions.prompt: A ticketing app commits a customer's purchase of two theatre seats. One second later, the data centre loses power. When the database restarts, the purchase is still recorded. Which ACID guarantee does this demonstrate?
choices: Consistency, because the seat count stayed within the database's rules.
Durability, because a committed change survived the power loss.
Isolation, because no other customer saw the purchase before it finished.
Atomicity, because both seats were saved together as one unit.
questions.why: Durability is the guarantee that once a change is committed it survives a crash or power loss.

questions.prompt: A clinic's appointment-booking database stores each patient's phone number once, in a Patients table, and appointments refer to the patient rather than repeating the number. What is this design called, and why does it suit a transactional workload?
choices: Normalization; each fact is stored once, so writes stay small and there are no conflicting copies.
Normalization; copying the phone number into every appointment makes reads faster for reports.
Isolation; splitting data into tables stops concurrent bookings from seeing each other's work.
Durability; storing the number in one table ensures it survives if the server crashes.
questions.why: Normalized data is split into related tables so each fact is stored once, which keeps writes small and avoids conflicting copies of the same fact.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what makes a workload transactional and why ACID matters. Then name one tradeoff or limit of a transactional design, for example why it is a poor fit for large reporting queries.
lessons.modelAnswer: A transactional, or OLTP, workload records business events as they happen. Think of orders, payments and bookings. It handles lots of small, quick reads and writes from many users at the same time, and every one has to be correct. It relies on ACID. Atomicity means each transaction fully happens or not at all. Consistency means the database's rules are never broken. Isolation means simultaneous transactions don't trip over each other. Durability means committed data survives a crash. For example, a transfer that crashes midway is rolled back, so no money disappears. The data is usually normalized into many related tables, which keeps writes small and avoids duplicate facts. The tradeoff is that normalization and strict guarantees suit small, current operations, not big reporting. Scanning years of history across many joined tables is slow, and it competes with live users. That kind of work belongs in a separate analytical system.
rubricPoints: Defines a transactional workload as recording live business events with many small, fast reads and writes from many users at once.
Explains that a transaction is a single unit of work that ends in a commit or a rollback.
Names and briefly explains atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.
Mentions that the data is typically normalized to keep writes small and avoid duplicate facts.
Names a limit, such as being poorly suited to large historical or reporting queries, which belong in analytical workloads.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is recognizing a transactional workload from a short scenario and telling it apart from an analytical one, so reasoning through exam-style situations helps most.

lessons.plain: An analytical workload is the kind of data work that looks back over lots of records to answer questions and spot trends, rather than recording each new event as it happens. Think of a shop. The till ringing up each sale is the everyday recording. At the end of the month, the owner reads through all the receipts to ask which products sold best, on which days, and in which branch. That second activity is analytical: mostly reading, over large amounts of history, summarising into totals and averages. It usually runs on a copy of the data that has been cleaned and organised for questions, not on the busy system taking orders.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop records every sale as it happens, and once a quarter a manager asks for total sales by region for the past three years. Which of those two jobs do you think touches more rows at once, and why might it be a bad idea to run it on the same system that is taking customers' orders?
lessons.teach:
An analytical workload is processing whose purpose is to read large volumes of mostly historical data and summarise it into insight such as totals, averages, trends and comparisons. Its typical features are that it is read-heavy (data is loaded in batches, then queried many times, rarely updated row by row), each query scans many rows but often only a few columns, results are aggregated (combined into sums, counts or averages), and a short delay before new data appears is usually acceptable.

Why is it organised this way? Answering a business question means looking across history, so the data is gathered from operational systems, cleaned, and loaded into a separate analytical store. A data warehouse is such a store: a database designed for querying structured historical data. A data lake is a cheaper file store holding raw files of many kinds for later analysis. Analytical data is often denormalised, meaning related information is deliberately copied into fewer, wider tables so queries need fewer joins. It is often stored by column, so a query reading two columns skips the rest. The step that moves and reshapes the data is ETL (extract, transform, load) or ELT (load first, then transform).

Worked example: a retailer wants monthly revenue per region for three years. First, each night a pipeline extracts the day's orders from the sales database. Second, it transforms them, fixing region codes and adding a month column. Third, it loads them into the warehouse. Fourth, an analyst's query reads millions of rows but only the region, month and amount columns. Fifth, it groups them and sums the amounts, returning 36 months of totals per region for a report.

A common mistake is running heavy analytical queries directly against the live transactional database. Those long scans compete for the same disk, memory and processor capacity as customer orders, so checkout slows or times out for real users. Keeping analysis on a separate store protects the operational system, at the cost that reports show data as of the last load rather than this second.

questions.prompt: A city bus company wants the average delay in minutes per route for each week of the past two years. Step 1: each night a pipeline extracts the day's trip records from the live ticketing and tracking system. Step 2: it transforms them, calculating a delay-minutes value for each trip and adding a week column. Step 3: it loads the cleaned records into the company's data warehouse. Step 4: ??? Step 5: the results are grouped by route and week and the delays are averaged, giving 104 weekly figures per route for a planning report. Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: A query scans several million trip rows but reads only the route, week and delay-minutes columns
Each trip row in the warehouse is updated one at a time as buses report their positions
A planner queries the live tracking system directly so the averages include trips still running right now
A query looks up one trip by its ID and returns every column for that single journey
questions.why: An analytical query typically scans many rows while reading only the few columns it needs, which then feed the grouping and averaging in Step 5.

questions.prompt: A streaming music service stores its listening history for analysis. Instead of keeping songs, artists and genres in separate linked tables, it copies the artist name and genre into one wide listening table, and it stores that table by column. What is the main benefit of this design for analytical queries?
choices: Each new listen can be inserted and corrected row by row faster than in the live system
The data no longer needs to be extracted from the operational systems
Reports always show plays that happened in the last second
Queries need fewer joins, and a query using only a few columns can skip the rest
questions.why: Denormalising (copying related information into fewer, wider tables) cuts joins, and column storage lets a query read only the columns it needs.

questions.prompt: Which of these workloads is analytical rather than transactional?
choices: An airline system that reserves seat 14C when a passenger books and updates it if they change seats
A pharmacy till that records each sale and reduces the stock count for that item
A gym chain comparing total memberships sold per branch over the last five years, refreshed weekly
A bank app that deducts money from one account and adds it to another during a transfer
questions.why: Summarising years of history into totals per branch, with a delay of a week being acceptable, is read-heavy and aggregated, which marks it as analytical.

questions.prompt: An online ticket seller lets its analysts run large year-over-year sales reports directly against the same live database that handles ticket purchases. What problem is most likely?
choices: Purchases slow down or time out, because the long report scans compete for the same disk, memory and processor capacity
The database will automatically copy the data into a data lake and stop accepting orders
The reports will be less accurate because a live database cannot calculate sums
The reports will only show data as of the last nightly load
questions.why: Heavy analytical scans share resources with customer transactions on the live system, so real buyers experience slowdowns; a separate analytical store avoids this.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what makes a workload analytical rather than everyday record-keeping, and name one tradeoff of moving analysis onto a separate store such as a data warehouse.
lessons.modelAnswer: An analytical workload exists to answer questions about the past, like which region grew fastest last year, rather than to record each sale or booking as it happens. It reads far more than it writes. Data arrives in batches through an ETL or ELT pipeline, and each query scans huge numbers of rows, usually only a few columns, and boils them down into sums, counts or averages. To make that fast, the data is copied into a separate store like a data warehouse or data lake, often denormalised into wide tables and stored by column. The big benefit is that heavy reports no longer slow down the live system customers use. The tradeoff is freshness: the warehouse only knows what the last load brought in, so reports may be hours behind. You also have to build and run the pipeline that keeps the copy in step.
rubricPoints: States that analytical workloads summarise large amounts of historical data into insight such as totals and trends.
Notes they are read-heavy, loaded in batches and rarely updated row by row.
Mentions queries scan many rows, often few columns, and aggregate results.
Names a separate analytical store such as a data warehouse or data lake fed by ETL or ELT.
Names a tradeoff such as data latency or the cost of maintaining the pipeline.
Explains the risk of running heavy analytical queries on the live transactional system.

suggested.rationale: Writing aggregate queries that group and sum many rows of historical data in a SQL lab lets the learner see the read-heavy, summarising shape of an analytical workload directly.

lessons.plain: A database administrator, or DBA, is the person who keeps an organization's databases running, safe and recoverable. Think of a building superintendent: they don't decide what tenants do in their apartments, but they make sure the doors lock, the heating works, keys go only to the right people, and there is a plan if a pipe bursts. A DBA does the same for databases. They install and configure the database system, decide who may read or change data, take backups and practise restoring them, apply updates, and watch performance so the database stays fast and available for everyone who depends on it.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop's order database was accidentally wiped at 3 a.m. Whose job was it to make sure the data could be brought back, and what would that person have needed to do beforehand?
lessons.teach:
A database administrator (DBA) is responsible for the operation of databases: keeping them available, secure, performing well and recoverable. A database here means an organized store of data managed by software called a database management system.

The main responsibilities are these. Availability means the database is up when people need it; the DBA plans for failures, for example with a standby copy that can take over. Security means controlling access through authentication (proving who you are) and authorization (what you are then allowed to do), and protecting sensitive data, for example with encryption, which scrambles data so only key holders can read it. Backup and recovery means taking regular copies and, crucially, testing that they restore. Patching means applying vendor updates that fix bugs and security holes. Performance monitoring means watching speed and resource use and tuning slow queries (requests for data) or adding indexes, which are lookup structures that speed up finding rows.

Why a separate role? Other people use the data; someone must own the health of the system itself, or nobody does. In Azure, managed services such as Azure SQL Database automate parts of this, like patching and automatic backups, but the DBA still decides access, retention and recovery settings.

Worked example: a developer deletes the customers table at 10:15. The DBA checks the backup policy, finds point-in-time restore is enabled, restores the database to 10:14 as a new copy, verifies the row counts, and then recovers the lost table. Afterward the DBA removes delete rights the developer did not need.

A common mistake is confusing roles: the DBA does not build data pipelines (a data engineer's job) or build reports (a data analyst's job). Another mistake is treating backups as done because they run; an untested backup may fail exactly when needed, turning a short outage into permanent data loss.

questions.prompt: A logistics company stores shipment records in a database. Drivers complain that the 'find shipment by tracking number' screen now takes 40 seconds to load. The DBA works through it. Step 1: the DBA checks performance monitoring and sees this one query using most of the server's CPU. Step 2: the DBA finds that the query reads every one of the 8 million rows to find a single tracking number. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the DBA reruns the query, sees it now finishes in under a second, and keeps monitoring it over the next week. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Add an index on the tracking number column so matching rows can be found without reading the whole table
Remove the drivers' read access so the query stops running and frees up the CPU
Ask a data engineer to build a pipeline that copies shipment records into a separate store
Restore the database from last night's backup so the table returns to a faster state
questions.why: An index is a lookup structure that speeds up finding rows, which fixes a query that reads every row to find one match. Restoring a backup, building a pipeline or blocking access would not make the lookup itself faster.

questions.prompt: A regional bookstore chain has several data tasks this month. Which one is the database administrator's responsibility?
choices: Giving a new auditor read-only access to the sales database and making sure card details are encrypted
Designing a dashboard that shows the top-selling books by region
Building a pipeline that pulls daily sales files from each store into a central data store
Writing a summary of buying trends for the marketing team
questions.why: Controlling access and protecting sensitive data are security duties of the DBA. Pipelines belong to a data engineer, and dashboards and trend analysis belong to a data analyst.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, the database backups have run automatically every night for 14 months, and every job reports 'success'. Nobody has ever tried restoring one. What is the main risk?
choices: There is no real risk, because a backup that reports success is guaranteed to restore
A backup may turn out to be unusable when it is actually needed, so a short outage could become permanent data loss
The nightly backup jobs will slowly make queries slower until the database stops working
Backups that are never restored expire automatically after 12 months, so the older copies are already gone
questions.why: A backup only proves its value when it restores. Without testing, it may fail at the worst moment, which turns a recoverable incident into lost data.

questions.prompt: A small travel startup moves its booking database to Azure SQL Database, a managed relational database service that handles patching and automatic backups. Which responsibility still stays with the startup's DBA?
choices: Applying the vendor's security updates by hand every month
Nothing, because a managed service takes over every DBA duty
Deciding who can access the data, how long backups are kept, and how recovery is set up
Starting each nightly backup job by hand
questions.why: Managed services automate parts of the work, such as patching and backups, but the DBA still decides access, retention and recovery settings.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a database administrator is responsible for, how it differs from a data engineer and a data analyst, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on a managed cloud database to handle DBA tasks.
lessons.modelAnswer: A DBA owns the health of the database itself: keeping it available, secure, fast and recoverable. That means managing who can log in and what they may do, protecting sensitive data, scheduling backups and testing restores, applying patches, and monitoring and tuning performance. A data engineer instead builds pipelines that move and transform data between systems, and a data analyst turns data into reports and insights; both rely on the DBA's databases working. On Azure, a managed service like Azure SQL Database automates patching and backups, which saves effort, but it doesn't remove the role: someone still has to grant the right permissions, pick backup retention, and actually practise a restore. The tradeoff is less control over things like update timing in exchange for less manual work, and automation can create false confidence if nobody verifies recovery.
rubricPoints: States the DBA manages database availability, security, backups and recovery, patching, and performance.
Mentions controlling access through authentication and authorization.
Notes backups must be tested by restoring, not just taken.
Distinguishes DBA from data engineer (pipelines) and data analyst (reports).
Names a limit of managed services, such as permissions and recovery decisions still needing a person.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests recognizing which tasks belong to a DBA versus other data roles, so explaining the role boundaries back is the core skill and no mission exercises database administration directly.

lessons.plain: A data engineer is the person who builds and looks after the pipes that move data around an organisation. Data starts out scattered: sales in one system, website clicks in another, spreadsheets on someone's laptop. The data engineer collects it, cleans it up, reshapes it into a consistent form, and delivers it to a central place where others can use it. They also keep those pipes running reliably and securely. Think of a city water department. It does not drink the water or decide what to cook. It brings water in from rivers, treats it, and makes sure clean water reaches every tap on time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop's sales system, its website, and its warehouse spreadsheet all record orders in different formats. Before an analyst can build one report from all three, someone has to gather and tidy that data. What steps do you think that person needs to take?
lessons.teach:
A data engineer designs, builds and maintains the systems that move data from where it is created to where it is analysed. Their core work is the data pipeline. A pipeline is an automated, repeatable series of steps that copies, transforms and loads data.

The classic pattern is ETL: extract, transform, load. Extract means pulling data out of source systems, such as a transactional database or files. Transform means cleaning and reshaping it, for example fixing date formats, removing duplicates or joining tables. Load means writing the result into an analytical store, such as a data warehouse (a database organised for reporting) or a data lake (cheap storage that holds raw files of any format). A variant is ELT, where data is loaded first and transformed inside the store. On Azure, a service such as Azure Data Factory, a managed pipeline orchestration service, often runs these steps.

Data engineers also own data quality, scheduling, monitoring pipeline runs, and applying security and privacy rules to the data as it moves. This works because analysts need data that is consistent, complete and up to date, and doing that by hand every day does not scale.

Worked example: a retailer wants a daily sales dashboard. The pipeline runs at 2 a.m. and works through four steps. First, it extracts yesterday's orders from the store database and the web shop's JSON export. Second, it converts currencies to one currency, standardises product codes and drops test orders. Third, it loads the clean rows into a warehouse sales table. Fourth, it logs success, or raises an alert if a source was missing.

A common mistake is to confuse the data engineer with neighbouring roles. The database administrator keeps a database itself healthy, handling backups, performance, access and availability. The data analyst explores the prepared data and builds reports and visualisations. The data engineer sits between them and moves and prepares the data.

If pipelines fail silently, dashboards show stale or wrong numbers, and business decisions are made on bad data.

questions.prompt: A city bus company wants a weekly ridership report. A data engineer builds a pipeline that runs every Sunday at 1 a.m. Step 1: it extracts last week's card taps from the fare system database and the CSV files uploaded by the buses' GPS units. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: it loads the resulting rows into a ridership table in the data warehouse, a database organised for reporting. Step 4: it logs success, or raises an alert if the GPS files did not arrive. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Take a backup of the fare system database and tune its indexes so queries run faster
Build a bar chart of riders per route for the weekly management meeting
Copy the raw GPS files into a data lake, unchanged, so they can be read later
Convert all timestamps to one time zone, remove duplicate taps and join each tap to its route ID
questions.why: Step 2 sits between extract and load, so it is the transform step, which cleans and reshapes the data by fixing formats, removing duplicates and joining tables.

questions.prompt: An energy company copies raw smart-meter reading files straight into a data lake, which is cheap storage for raw files of any format. It then runs the cleaning and reshaping inside the lake afterwards. What is this pipeline pattern called?
choices: Database administration, because it keeps the storage healthy
Data visualisation, because the readings end up in a report
ETL, because the data is extracted and transformed before it is loaded
ELT, because the data is loaded first and transformed inside the store
questions.why: ELT is the variant where data is loaded into the store first and transformed there. In ETL, the transform step happens before the load.

questions.prompt: A university has a data engineer, a database administrator and a data analyst. Which task belongs to the data engineer?
choices: Granting a new staff member access to the student records database
Building a scheduled pipeline that copies enrolment data into the warehouse nightly and alerts on failure
Designing a dashboard of enrolment trends for the deans to review each term
Restoring the student records database from last night's backup after a disk failure
questions.why: The data engineer builds and monitors automated pipelines that move and prepare data. Backups and database access belong to the database administrator, and dashboards belong to the data analyst.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's nightly pipeline stopped loading new shipment data three days ago. No alert was raised. What is the most likely result?
choices: The shipments dashboard keeps showing out-of-date figures, and managers make decisions on stale data
The source shipment database deletes its records because they were never copied
The dashboard shows an error message and stops displaying anything
The data warehouse notices the gap and pulls the missing shipments by itself
questions.why: When a pipeline fails silently, the analytical store simply stops receiving new data. Reports then look normal but show stale or wrong numbers, which is why data engineers monitor runs and raise alerts.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a data engineer is responsible for, how that differs from a database administrator and a data analyst, and name one tradeoff or limit in how pipelines deliver data.
lessons.modelAnswer: A data engineer builds and runs the pipelines that get data from the systems where it is created into a store built for analysis. They extract data from sources like transactional databases and files, transform it by cleaning, deduplicating and standardising it, and load it into a data warehouse or data lake. They also schedule and monitor those pipelines, check data quality, and apply security and privacy rules along the way. A database administrator, by contrast, keeps a database itself running, handling backups, performance and permissions. A data analyst uses the prepared data to find insights and build reports. One tradeoff is freshness versus cost and complexity. A nightly batch pipeline is simple and cheap, but the data is up to a day old. Near-real-time pipelines give fresher data but are harder to build and run, so engineers pick based on what the business actually needs.
rubricPoints: Defines the data engineer as the person who builds and maintains data pipelines.
Describes extract, transform and load, or the ELT variant.
Names a destination such as a data warehouse or data lake.
Mentions ongoing duties like monitoring, data quality or security.
Distinguishes the role from the database administrator and the data analyst.
States a tradeoff, such as data freshness versus pipeline cost and complexity.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests telling the three data roles apart, and explaining that boundary in your own words is the core skill, and no listed mission targets it.

lessons.plain: A data analyst is the person who turns stored data into answers people can act on. They explore the numbers, find patterns and trends, and present what they find as reports, charts and dashboards that managers and colleagues can read without technical help. Think of a translator at a meeting: the data speaks a language of rows and columns, the business speaks in questions like 'why did sales drop in March?', and the analyst sits between them, making each understandable to the other. They usually work with data that others have already collected and stored.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sales manager asks, 'Which region's sales fell last quarter, and can I see that on a chart every Monday?' Who on a data team do you think takes that request, and what would they hand back?
lessons.teach:
A data analyst is the role responsible for exploring data, finding meaning in it, and communicating that meaning visually so the business can make decisions. On the DP-900 exam, this is one of three core data roles, alongside the database administrator, who keeps databases running, and the data engineer, who builds the systems that move and prepare data.

An analyst's main duties are: exploring data to find patterns and trends; light cleansing, meaning fixing or removing errors, duplicates and blanks that would distort a result; building a data model, which is a description of how tables relate to one another so they can be combined in a report; and producing visualizations, meaning charts, reports (pages of visuals on one topic) and dashboards (a single-screen summary that refreshes as data changes). Analysts often track KPIs, or key performance indicators, which are the few numbers a business watches to judge success, such as monthly revenue. In Azure, the analyst's main tool is Power BI, a business-intelligence service for modelling and visualizing data.

This works because decision-makers rarely read raw tables; a well-chosen chart shows a trend in seconds.

Worked example: the sales manager wants to know which region fell last quarter. Step one, the analyst connects Power BI to the sales data the engineers have already loaded into an analytical store.
