If the job needs many-table joins, strict relational reporting, or cheap storage of large files such as videos, a relational database or Blob storage fits better. The consequence in a running system is a high bill paid for scale you do not use, plus awkward queries that are slow or expensive.

questions.prompt: A language-learning mobile app has 3 million users spread across Asia, Europe and South America. The team checks whether Azure Cosmos DB fits. Step 1: user settings differ, since some learners save study goals and reminder times while others save only a nickname, so a flexible schema helps. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: launching a new course triples traffic overnight, so spreading data across partitions keyed by user ID lets throughput grow. Step 4: each screen loads one learner's profile by its user ID, a simple lookup. Which statement completes Step 2?
choices: Users are on one continent, so a single copy of the data is enough and no extra regions are needed.
Users are on three continents, so live copies of the data in several Azure regions let each user read from the nearest one and wait less.
Users are on three continents, so profile data should move to Blob storage, which is the cheapest place to keep it.
Users are on three continents, so splitting profiles into many related tables that are joined on every read will cut wait time.
questions.why: Global distribution replicates data to several regions so far-apart users read from a nearby copy, which matches users on three continents.

questions.prompt: In Azure Cosmos DB, what is a partition?
choices: A live copy of the whole database kept in another Azure region for nearby reads.
A backup that Azure takes automatically because the service is managed.
A slice of the data grouped by a chosen key, such as a device ID, that lets throughput and storage grow.
The fixed list of fields that every record in a container must have.
questions.why: Partitions are slices of data grouped by a chosen key, and spreading data across them is how Cosmos DB scales elastically.

questions.prompt: Which of these workloads is the best fit for Azure Cosmos DB?
choices: A legal office storing 5 TB of scanned contract PDFs that are rarely opened.
An accounting team building a monthly report that joins nine related tables with strict relational rules.
A film studio archiving 300 high-resolution video files as cheaply as possible.
A water utility whose 200,000 smart meters each send a small reading every minute.
questions.why: Many devices constantly writing small readings is an IoT and telemetry workload, which fits Cosmos DB's low latency and elastic scale, while large files and multi-table joins fit Blob storage or a relational database.

questions.prompt: A regional insurance firm with steady traffic in one country picks Azure Cosmos DB for its claims reporting, which joins policy, customer, claim and payment tables every month. What is the most likely result in the running system?
choices: The firm pays a high bill for scale it does not use, and the multi-table reporting queries are awkward, slow or expensive.
Nothing changes, because Cosmos DB and a relational database suit the same workloads.
Costs drop because the flexible schema removes the need to define any fields.
Reports become faster because Cosmos DB answers every query in single-digit milliseconds regardless of joins.
questions.why: Choosing Cosmos DB for many-table joins and strict relational reporting leads to paying for unused scale and awkward, slow or expensive queries, so a relational database fits better.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, when Azure Cosmos DB is a good choice for a new application, and name one situation where it is the wrong tool and why.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cosmos DB is Azure's managed NoSQL database. Data is usually stored as JSON documents, so records do not all need the same fields. I'd pick it when an app needs very fast reads and writes for users in many places, because it can keep replicas in several regions and answer in a few milliseconds. It also scales out by splitting data into partitions by a key such as user ID, which handles traffic spikes. Good examples are IoT sensor streams, product catalogs with varied attributes, game player profiles and leaderboards, and user profiles or carts in web and mobile apps. It's the wrong tool for heavy relational reporting with many joins, where a relational database is simpler. It's also wrong for storing big files like videos, where Blob storage is cheaper. Using it there means paying for global scale you don't need.
rubricPoints: Defines Cosmos DB as a managed NoSQL database storing flexible, schema-free items such as JSON documents.
Links use cases to traits: global replication, low latency, elastic scale through partitions, and flexible schema.
Names concrete use cases such as IoT telemetry, retail catalogs, gaming, and web or mobile user data.
Names a poor fit such as complex relational joins and reporting, or large file storage.
Mentions the tradeoff of cost or awkward querying when it is used where it isn't needed.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests matching a described workload to the right data service, so reasoning through short scenarios that weigh Cosmos DB against relational and Blob options builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Azure Cosmos DB is Microsoft's managed, globally distributed database for non-relational data, meaning data that does not have to fit fixed rows and columns. An API (application programming interface) is the 'language' your application uses to talk to the database. Cosmos DB offers several of these, so teams can keep the tools and code they already know. Think of a translator at an international desk who serves each visitor in their own language. The engine behind the desk stays the same, but each visitor uses the language they already speak. Picking the right API means matching the data shape and the team's existing skills.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team already runs an app on MongoDB and wants to move it to Azure Cosmos DB while changing as little code as possible. Which Cosmos DB API do you think they should pick, and why?
lessons.teach:
An Azure Cosmos DB API is the interface and data model an account exposes. You choose one API when you create the account, and it fixes how data is stored and queried in that account. The API cannot be changed later. Underneath, the same managed service supplies the shared benefits: global replication (copies of data in many regions), elastic scaling, and low response times.

The APIs you should know are these. API for NoSQL is the native option. It stores JSON documents, which are self-describing records made of fields and values, and you query them with a SQL-like language. It is the default for new apps. API for MongoDB speaks the MongoDB wire protocol, so existing MongoDB drivers and code work with little change. API for Apache Cassandra uses a column-family model: rows in tables where each row can hold different columns. It is queried with CQL (Cassandra Query Language) and suits teams that already use Cassandra. API for Apache Gremlin stores graphs. A graph is made of vertices (entities) and edges (relationships), and it fits highly connected data such as social networks or recommendation engines. API for Table stores key-value entities and is a drop-in upgrade path for apps written against Azure Table storage. API for PostgreSQL is the exception because it is relational. It is distributed PostgreSQL for scaling out SQL workloads.

Worked example: a retailer wants to suggest products based on 'customers who bought X also bought Y'. Step 1: what is the data shape? Mostly relationships between customers and products. Step 2: which model handles relationships best? A graph. Step 3: choose the API for Apache Gremlin.

Common mistake: answering 'Cosmos DB' and stopping there, or picking API for NoSQL by habit when the scenario mentions existing Cassandra, MongoDB, or Table storage code. Those clues point to the compatible API. In a running system, a wrong pick means rewriting data access code or migrating to a new account, because the API is locked once the account exists.

questions.prompt: A courier company runs a parcel-tracking app that was written against Azure Table storage. Each record is a simple key-value entity: a depot code plus a parcel ID as the key, and a handful of properties such as status and weight. About 60,000 records are stored today, and the company wants global replication and low response times without rewriting its data access code. Step 1: what is the data shape? Simple key-value entities. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: choose the Azure Cosmos DB API for Table. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Note that the API can be switched later, so code compatibility does not matter at this stage.
Note that API for NoSQL is the default for new apps, so it should be the starting point here.
Note that depots and parcels are related to each other, so a graph model is the better fit.
Note that the existing code targets Azure Table storage, so the compatible API avoids a rewrite.
questions.why: The clue that the app already targets Azure Table storage points to API for Table, which is the drop-in upgrade path and avoids rewriting data access code.

questions.prompt: A team created an Azure Cosmos DB account with API for NoSQL. Six months later, they decide they want to query the same account using CQL (Cassandra Query Language). What is true?
choices: The API cannot be changed, so they would need a new account using API for Apache Cassandra and a data migration.
They only need to add a Cassandra driver; the account adapts automatically.
CQL queries work on any Cosmos DB account, whichever API it was created with.
They can switch the existing account to API for Apache Cassandra in the account settings.
questions.why: The API is fixed when the account is created, so changing to Cassandra means creating a new account and migrating the data.

questions.prompt: A mobile game studio is moving its player-profile service to Azure. The service already uses MongoDB drivers and queries throughout its code, and the studio wants to change as little code as possible. Which Azure Cosmos DB API fits best?
choices: API for Table, because player profiles are simple records
API for Apache Gremlin, because players connect to each other
API for MongoDB, because it speaks the MongoDB wire protocol
API for NoSQL, because it is the native default for new apps
questions.why: API for MongoDB accepts the MongoDB wire protocol, so the studio's existing drivers and code keep working with little change.

questions.prompt: A payroll provider has an existing relational database built on PostgreSQL. Its tables and SQL queries are growing too large for one server, and the provider wants to scale the workload out across many machines while keeping it relational. Which Azure Cosmos DB API fits?
choices: API for Apache Cassandra, because its tables are made of rows and columns
API for PostgreSQL, because it is distributed PostgreSQL for scaling out relational workloads
API for NoSQL, because it uses a SQL-like query language
API for Table, because payroll entries can be stored as keyed entities
questions.why: API for PostgreSQL is the one relational Cosmos DB API, offering distributed PostgreSQL for scaling out SQL workloads.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose among the Azure Cosmos DB APIs for a new project, and name one limit or tradeoff of that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cosmos DB is one managed, globally distributed engine that exposes several APIs, and I pick one per account. First I look at the data shape and at what the team already uses. For a new app with JSON documents, I'd choose API for NoSQL, the native option with SQL-like queries. If we're migrating MongoDB or Cassandra code, I'd choose the matching API so existing drivers and queries keep working. Highly connected data like social links or recommendations calls for Gremlin, the graph API. Simple key-value apps moving off Azure Table storage fit the Table API, and a relational workload that needs to scale out fits API for PostgreSQL. The tradeoff is that the API is fixed when the account is created. If we choose wrong, we'll have to migrate data to a new account and rewrite our data access code.
rubricPoints: Cosmos DB is one managed engine that exposes multiple APIs, each with its own data model.
The API is chosen per account at creation and cannot be changed afterward.
NoSQL means native JSON documents queried with SQL-like syntax, and is the default for new apps.
MongoDB, Cassandra, and Table APIs let existing apps migrate with minimal code change.
Gremlin is for graph data with vertices and edges, and PostgreSQL is the relational, distributed option.
A wrong choice forces a data migration and code rewrite.

suggested.rationale: Choosing an API comes down to reading scenario clues about data shape and existing tools, so working through exam-style situations builds the skill best, and no mission or planned engine covers Cosmos DB.

lessons.plain: Before anyone can analyse data, it has to be gathered from the places it is created, such as sales databases, files and devices, and moved somewhere built for analysis. Gathering and moving it is called ingestion. Cleaning and reshaping it so it is useful is called processing. Think of a restaurant kitchen. Deliveries arrive from many suppliers (ingestion), then cooks wash, chop and combine the ingredients (processing) before anything reaches a plate. Planning this well means asking four things. Where does the data come from? How much is there? How fresh does it need to be? How much cleaning does it need?
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop wants yesterday's sales in a report every morning, and its sales database grows by millions of rows a year. Would you copy the whole database every night, or only the rows that changed since the last copy? Why?
lessons.teach:
Data ingestion means copying data from source systems into an analytics environment. A source system is wherever data is produced, such as an order database, CSV files or sensors. Processing means cleaning and reshaping that data so it can be queried. Typical processing steps fix data types, remove duplicates, join tables and summarise.

Both jobs usually run inside a pipeline. A pipeline is a defined, repeatable series of steps, called activities, that starts on a schedule or when an event happens. Azure Data Factory is a managed orchestration service, meaning it coordinates when and in what order the steps run. Pipelines in Azure Synapse Analytics and Microsoft Fabric work the same way. They reach many sources through connectors, which are built-in adapters for each kind of system. They move the data and then call compute to transform it.

There are two common patterns. In ETL (extract, transform, load), data is cleaned while it is moving, so only finished data is loaded. In ELT (extract, load, transform), raw data is landed first, usually in a data lake. A data lake is low-cost storage for large volumes of files in any format. The data is then transformed using the analytical store's own power. ELT keeps a raw copy, so you can reprocess the data when business rules change.

The key considerations are the source and its format, the volume, the required freshness (latency), how complex the transformations are, and whether to load incrementally. An incremental load copies only new or changed rows. It uses a watermark to find them, which is a saved marker such as the last-modified time of the previous run.

Here is a worked example. Step 1: at 01:00 a schedule trigger starts the pipeline. Step 2: a copy activity reads sales rows modified after the stored watermark. Step 3: the raw rows land in the data lake. Step 4: a transform step removes duplicates, converts currencies and adds product names. Step 5: the clean data loads into the analytical store, and the watermark moves forward. Step 6: the morning report reads fresh totals.

A common mistake is reloading the entire source every night "to be safe". As the data grows, each run takes longer and costs more. It also adds heavy load to the production database that customers depend on, until the job no longer finishes before business hours.

questions.prompt: A bike-rental company copies ride records from its booking database into an analytics environment every hour, using an incremental load. The previous run saved a watermark of 05:00, meaning the latest last-modified time it had copied. Here is the 06:00 run. Step 1: a schedule trigger starts the pipeline at 06:00. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the 4,200 rows that were picked up land unchanged as files in the data lake. Step 4: a transform step converts text dates into real date values and removes duplicate rides. Step 5: the clean rows load into the analytical store, and the newest last-modified time from this run is saved as the new watermark. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: A copy activity reads every ride row in the booking database, so that nothing is missed
A copy activity reads only the ride rows whose last-modified time is after the 05:00 watermark
A transform step cleans the ride rows inside the booking database before anything is copied
A copy activity reads only the ride rows whose last-modified time is after 06:00 today
questions.why: An incremental load uses the saved watermark from the previous run (05:00) to find and copy only the rows that are new or changed since then.

questions.prompt: A retailer lands raw point-of-sale files in a data lake and only then transforms them using the analytical store's own compute. Six months later, the finance team changes how it defines a 'returned' sale. What advantage does this ELT pattern give the retailer?
choices: Only finished data was ever loaded, so no reprocessing is possible or needed
Connectors are no longer required to reach the point-of-sale system
A raw copy of the data is kept, so the history can be reprocessed under the new rule
The pipeline no longer needs a schedule or an event to start it
questions.why: ELT lands the raw data first, so it can be transformed again when business rules change, while ETL loads only finished data.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm loads shipment records incrementally. After last night's run, the stored watermark is 2024-03-10 18:00, which is the last-modified time of the newest row that run copied. Which rows should the next run copy?
choices: Only rows that the previous run failed to remove as duplicates
Only rows that are new or have been changed after 2024-03-10 18:00
Every shipment row in the source table, whatever its last-modified time
Only rows created before 2024-03-10 18:00, since those are already confirmed
questions.why: A watermark marks where the previous run stopped, so an incremental load copies only the rows that are new or changed after that point.

questions.prompt: A warehouse company reloads its whole inventory database into the analytics store every night 'to be safe', and the database grows each month. What is the most likely consequence over time?
choices: Runs become faster each month, because the pipeline learns which rows have changed
Each run takes longer, costs more and puts heavy load on the production database, until it no longer finishes before business hours
The data lake stops accepting files, because it can only store data in one format
The morning reports gain lower latency, because more data is copied on every run
questions.why: A full reload copies everything on every run, so as the data grows, run time, cost and load on the production source all grow with it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would plan getting data from an operational database into an analytics store. Cover ETL versus ELT and incremental loading, and name one tradeoff of your choices.
lessons.modelAnswer: Ingestion copies data out of the systems that create it. Processing cleans and reshapes it for analysis. A pipeline, for example in Azure Data Factory or Fabric, runs these steps on a schedule or trigger. First I'd check the source and its format, how much data there is, how fresh the reports need to be, and how much transformation is needed. With ETL you transform in flight and load only clean data. With ELT you land the raw data in a data lake first and transform it there. ELT keeps a raw copy you can reprocess, but you must store and govern that raw data. I'd load incrementally, using a watermark such as a last-modified time so only changed rows move. That keeps runs short and protects the production database. The tradeoff is extra complexity. If the watermark is wrong, rows can be skipped or duplicated, so you need validation checks.
rubricPoints: Defines ingestion as moving data from sources and processing as cleaning and reshaping it.
Describes a pipeline as an orchestrated, scheduled or triggered sequence of activities, such as in Azure Data Factory or Fabric.
Contrasts ETL with ELT and notes that ELT lands raw data in a data lake first.
Names the key considerations: source and format, volume, freshness or latency, and transformation complexity.
Explains incremental loading with a watermark and why full reloads do not scale.
States a tradeoff, such as raw-data storage cost or the risk of watermark errors.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through scenarios where you pick an ingestion pattern and pipeline approach, so reasoning through exam-style situations reinforces the considerations best.

lessons.plain: An analytical data store is a place where an organization keeps large amounts of historical data specifically so people can ask big summary questions of it, like total sales by region over five years. It is separate from the everyday databases that record each sale as it happens. Think of a shop's till receipts compared with the accountant's filing room: the till handles one purchase at a time, while the filing room is organized for looking across everything at once. The main options are a data warehouse (tidy tables), a data lake (raw files of any kind), and a lakehouse that blends the two.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants to keep years of sales figures in neat tables for monthly reports, and also wants to store millions of raw website click log files and product photos it may analyze later. Would you put both kinds of data in the same tidy table structure, or treat them differently? Why?
lessons.teach:
An analytical data store holds large volumes of mostly historical data, organized for reading and summarizing rather than for fast single-row updates. There are three common shapes.

A data warehouse is a relational database (data in tables of rows and columns, queried with SQL) designed for analysis. Data is cleaned and given a fixed structure before it is loaded, called schema-on-write. Warehouses usually use a star schema: a central fact table holds measurable events, such as each sale's amount, and links to dimension tables that describe context, such as product, store and date.

A data lake is a large, cheap file store that accepts data in any format, including CSV, JSON, logs, images, or Parquet (a column-based file format good for analytics). Structure is applied only when the data is read, called schema-on-read. On Azure, Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 provides this kind of storage.

A lakehouse keeps data as files in a lake but adds a table layer on top, often the Delta Lake format, so you can query those files with SQL like warehouse tables while keeping lake flexibility. Azure Synapse Analytics and Microsoft Fabric both offer warehouse and lake or lakehouse options.

Worked example: a manager asks for total revenue per region last quarter. Step 1, the query reads the sales fact table. Step 2, it joins each sale to the store dimension to find the region. Step 3, it joins to the date dimension and keeps only last quarter. Step 4, it sums amounts per region. The star schema makes these joins simple and fast.

A common mistake is treating a data lake as a place to dump anything with no organization or catalogue. Because nothing enforces structure, nobody can find or trust the data later, a state people call a data swamp, and reports built on it give inconsistent answers. Another mistake is running heavy reports directly on the live transactional database, which slows down the application that customers use.

questions.prompt: A music streaming company is choosing an analytical data store. Trace its reasoning. Step 1: the data arrives in mixed formats: JSON play events, CSV royalty files and album cover images. A store that accepts any file format cheaply is needed, so the data goes into a data lake such as Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2. Step 2: analysts also want to query play events with SQL as if they were warehouse tables, without first converting everything into a separate relational database. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the result is a lakehouse. The files stay flexible in the lake, and analysts can still run SQL over them. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Run the analysts' SQL reports directly on the live app database that records plays as they happen
Clean every file and load it into fixed relational tables before storing it (schema-on-write), replacing the lake
Leave the files with no catalogue or organization, since schema-on-read means structure never needs to be applied
Keep the files in the lake and add a table layer on top, such as the Delta Lake format, so the files can be queried like tables
questions.why: A lakehouse keeps data as files in a lake and adds a table layer such as Delta Lake on top, so those files can be queried with SQL while the lake stays flexible.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm cleans its shipment records and fits them into fixed tables of rows and columns before loading them into its analysis database. What is this approach called, and which kind of store does it describe?
choices: Schema-on-write, typical of a data warehouse
Schema-on-write, typical of a data lake
Schema-on-read, typical of a data warehouse
Schema-on-read, typical of a data lake
questions.why: In a data warehouse, data is given a fixed structure before it is loaded, and that approach is called schema-on-write.

questions.prompt: An airline designs a star schema to analyze ticket revenue. It has four tables: Route (origin and destination cities), Passenger (name and loyalty tier), Calendar (day, month and year), and Booking (one row per ticket sold, with the fare paid). Which table should be the central fact table?
choices: Passenger, because each ticket belongs to a person
Calendar, because every analysis filters by date
Booking, because it records each measurable event and its fare
Route, because every flight follows a route
questions.why: A fact table holds measurable events, here each ticket sold and its fare, while Route, Passenger and Calendar describe context and are dimension tables.

questions.prompt: For two years, a retailer's teams copied files into its data lake with no naming rules, no organization and no catalogue. Now two analysts build 'monthly returns' reports from the lake and get different totals. What has most likely happened?
choices: The lake has become a warehouse because it now holds too much data
Schema-on-read forces the data into fixed tables when it is loaded
The lake has become a data swamp, so nobody can find or trust the data
The star schema's dimension tables have been joined in the wrong order
questions.why: Nothing in a data lake enforces structure, so if data is dumped in with no organization or catalogue, it becomes a data swamp that people cannot find or trust, and reports built on it give inconsistent answers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a data warehouse, a data lake and a lakehouse, and say when you would pick each. Include one limit or tradeoff of each option.
lessons.modelAnswer: All three hold historical data for analysis, kept apart from the live transactional database so reports do not slow the app. A data warehouse stores cleaned data in relational tables, often a star schema with a fact table of events linked to dimension tables like product and date. Structure is enforced when loading, so it is reliable and fast for SQL reporting, but it is rigid and poor at raw or unstructured data. A data lake, such as Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, stores files of any format cheaply and applies structure only when read, so it suits raw logs, images and future data science; the tradeoff is that without discipline it becomes an untrustworthy data swamp. A lakehouse adds a table layer like Delta Lake over lake files, giving SQL querying with lake flexibility, at the cost of extra format and governance setup. Synapse and Fabric offer these options.
rubricPoints: Analytical stores hold large historical data for summarizing, separate from live transactional databases.
A data warehouse uses relational tables with schema-on-write, often a star schema of fact and dimension tables.
A data lake stores raw files of any format cheaply with schema-on-read, for example in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2.
A lakehouse adds a table layer such as Delta Lake over lake files so they can be queried like tables.
Names a tradeoff, such as warehouse rigidity or the risk of an unorganized data swamp.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right store for a described scenario, so reasoning through situations like structured reports versus raw files builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Large-scale analytics means crunching far more data than one computer can handle, such as years of sales records or billions of sensor readings, to find patterns and answer business questions. Microsoft offers cloud services that do this for you. Azure Databricks is a managed platform where data engineers and data scientists write code that is split across many machines working in parallel. Microsoft Fabric is an all-in-one analytics service where ingestion, storage, processing and reports live in one place. Think of a big kitchen: Databricks is a team of skilled chefs you direct, and Fabric is a full restaurant with every station under one roof.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you had ten years of shop sales records, far too large for one laptop, how might a cloud service finish a calculation like 'total sales per store per month' in minutes instead of days?
lessons.teach:
Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric are Microsoft cloud services for analyzing data at a scale beyond one machine.

Both rely on Apache Spark, an open-source engine that splits a large dataset into chunks and processes them in parallel on a cluster, which is a group of computers acting together. Splitting the work is why huge jobs finish quickly: ten machines each handle a tenth of the data at the same time.

Azure Databricks is a managed Spark platform. Managed means Azure creates and maintains the clusters for you. Users work in notebooks, which are documents that mix runnable code (Python, SQL, Scala or R) with notes and charts. It suits data engineering and machine learning, and it stores data in a lakehouse, which combines a data lake (cheap storage for raw files of any shape) with warehouse-style tables you can query with SQL.

Microsoft Fabric is a software-as-a-service analytics platform, meaning you sign in and use it without managing any servers. It bundles data ingestion pipelines, Spark data engineering, a lakehouse, a SQL data warehouse, real-time analytics, data science and Power BI reports. Everything shares OneLake, a single organization-wide data lake, so one copy of the data serves every tool.

Worked example: a retailer wants monthly sales per store from ten years of files. Step one, the files land in the lake. Step two, Spark divides them across cluster nodes. Step three, each node totals its chunk. Step four, partial totals are combined into one result table. Step five, the table feeds a report. Databricks would suit a code-first team running steps two to four; Fabric would run all five in one service.

A common mistake is thinking Databricks is a database or that Fabric is just Power BI. Databricks is a processing platform, and Fabric is a whole analytics suite. Picking based on that misunderstanding leads to a design with missing pieces, such as no place to store results or no way to report on them.

questions.prompt:
A regional hospital network stores 400 million appointment records in OneLake. It wants the average patient wait time for each clinic. The work runs through these steps.

Step 1: A Spark job splits the records into chunks across an 8-node cluster.
Step 2: Each node works only on its own chunk. For every clinic in that chunk, it adds up the wait minutes and counts the appointments.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The final per-clinic table feeds a Power BI report that hospital managers open each week.

Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: All 400 million records are copied back onto a single machine, which recalculates every clinic's wait time from scratch.
Power BI reopens the raw appointment files and recomputes the totals itself, ignoring the work the nodes already did.
Each node sends its own per-clinic averages straight to the report, so managers see eight separate figures for each clinic.
The partial sums and counts from all 8 nodes are combined per clinic, and the combined sum is divided by the combined count to give one average for each clinic.
questions.why: Spark gets its speed by having each node handle part of the data in parallel, and those partial results then have to be merged into one result table before a report can use it.

questions.prompt: A media company has 2 TB of video-view logs. It runs a Spark job on a 20-machine cluster. Why does the job finish far faster than it would on one machine?
choices: Spark compresses the 2 TB down to a size that one machine can read almost instantly.
Spark splits the data into chunks, so each of the 20 machines processes roughly a twentieth of the logs at the same time.
Each of the 20 machines processes the full 2 TB, and Spark keeps whichever copy finishes first.
Spark skips most of the logs and estimates the answer from a small sample.
questions.why: Apache Spark speeds up large jobs by dividing the dataset across the computers in a cluster and processing the pieces in parallel.

questions.prompt: A small charity has no IT staff. It wants to bring in donation data, store it, analyse it and build dashboards in one service. It does not want to manage any servers or clusters. Which option fits best?
choices: Azure Databricks on its own, because it is a database that also draws dashboards.
Power BI on its own, because Fabric and Power BI are the same product.
Microsoft Fabric, a software-as-a-service suite that bundles ingestion pipelines, a lakehouse, a warehouse and Power BI reports on shared storage.
A single large virtual machine running Spark, because a cluster is never needed for analytics.
questions.why: Fabric is software as a service, meaning you sign in without managing servers, and it covers ingestion, storage, analysis and reporting in one place.

questions.prompt: An architect plans a design using only Azure Databricks. The architect believes Databricks is a database and so expects it to handle everything, including business reports for executives. What is the flaw in this thinking?
choices: The flaw is that Databricks needs the organisation to build and maintain its own clusters by hand.
Databricks is a managed Spark processing platform, not a database, so the design may end up missing pieces such as a way to report on the results.
The flaw is that Databricks cannot run code at all, since it accepts only drag-and-drop dashboards.
There is no flaw, because Databricks is a relational database with a built-in reporting tool for executives.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that treating Databricks as a database misreads it as something other than a processing platform, and that this can leave a design with missing pieces such as no reporting layer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric each are, why they can process huge datasets quickly, and one tradeoff that would make you pick one over the other.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are Microsoft cloud services for analyzing data too big for one computer. They use Apache Spark, which splits the data across a cluster of machines so each handles a piece in parallel, then combines the results. Azure Databricks is a managed Spark platform: Azure runs the clusters, and engineers and data scientists write code in notebooks, storing results in a lakehouse that mixes raw-file storage with SQL tables. Microsoft Fabric is a software-as-a-service suite with no servers to manage. It bundles pipelines, Spark, lakehouse, warehouse, real-time analytics and Power BI on one shared lake called OneLake. The tradeoff: Databricks gives a code-first team deep control for engineering and machine learning but covers only part of the end-to-end flow, while Fabric gives everything in one place with less setup, which suits teams wanting a single integrated service including reporting.
rubricPoints: States both are cloud services for analyzing data at a scale beyond one machine.
Explains that Spark splits data across a cluster and processes the parts in parallel.
Describes Databricks as a managed, notebook-based Spark platform for engineering and machine learning.
Describes Fabric as an all-in-one software-as-a-service suite sharing OneLake and including Power BI.
Names a tradeoff such as code-first control versus end-to-end integration.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises these services directly, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that ask which service fits is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: Batch and streaming are two ways to handle data as it builds up over time. Batch processing means you collect data for a while and then process the whole pile in one go, on a schedule, such as every night. Streaming means you process each new piece of data within moments of it arriving, without waiting for a pile to form. Think of mail. Batch is emptying your mailbox once a day and reading everything together. Streaming is a phone notification for each message the second it lands. Neither is better in general. The right choice depends on how quickly someone needs the answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop wants two things: a report of yesterday's total sales, ready each morning, and an alert within seconds when one card is used in two countries at the same time. Which of these needs data processed the moment it arrives, and which can wait and be processed in one big run?
lessons.teach:
Batch processing collects data records over a period of time and then processes them together as one group, called a batch. The run usually happens on a schedule (nightly, hourly) or once a set amount of data has built up. Streaming processing, also called stream processing, handles each event shortly after it happens. An event is a single record of something occurring, such as a click, a sensor reading or a payment. A stream has no natural end, so streaming systems often group events into windows. A window is a short slice of time, such as 'the last 30 seconds', used to calculate running results like counts or averages.

The key tradeoff is latency against simplicity and cost. Latency is the delay between an event happening and its result being available. Batch has high latency, often hours, but it can process huge volumes efficiently and run complex calculations over complete data. Streaming has low latency, seconds or less, but each calculation sees only recent data, and the system must run continuously.

Worked example: a card payment arrives at 14:00:05. In a nightly batch design, it is stored. At 02:00 the job reads all of the day's payments, totals them, and writes the morning sales report. In a streaming design, the same payment is checked at 14:00:06 against the last five minutes of activity on that card. A purchase from another country inside that window raises a fraud alert immediately.

A common mistake is to assume streaming is always the modern, better choice. Choosing streaming for a monthly finance report adds always-on cost and complexity for no benefit. The opposite mistake also hurts a running system. If fraud detection runs as a nightly batch, the fraud is found many hours after the money has gone. Many real designs combine both approaches, streaming for instant alerts and batch for complete, accurate historical totals.

questions.prompt: A city water utility has pressure sensors on its pipes. Each sensor sends a reading every 5 seconds, and engineers want a burst-pipe alert within seconds if the average pressure over the last 60 seconds drops below a safe level. They choose a streaming design. Here is how one reading is traced. Step 1: A sensor reading arrives at 08:42:15. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: The new average is below the safe level, so a burst-pipe alert goes to the on-call engineer at 08:42:16. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: The system waits until one million readings have built up, then processes them together as one group.
The reading is added to every reading the sensor has ever sent, and the average since installation is recalculated.
The reading is added to a window covering the last 60 seconds (08:41:15 to 08:42:15), and the average pressure for that window is recalculated.
The reading is stored, and a job at 01:00 the next morning reads all of the day's readings and calculates the average pressure.
questions.why: Streaming handles each event shortly after it arrives and uses a short time window, here the last 60 seconds, to calculate running results like an average, which allows an alert within about a second.

questions.prompt: In data processing, what does the term latency mean?
choices: The short slice of time, such as the last 30 seconds, used to calculate running results.
The total amount of data a system can store before it needs more disk space.
The delay between an event happening and its result being available.
The number of records collected together and processed as one group.
questions.why: Latency is the delay from an event occurring to its result being ready; batch usually has high latency (hours) and streaming has low latency (seconds or less).

questions.prompt: A university wants a report, produced once at the end of each semester, showing the average grade in every course across all 40,000 students. Results are not needed until the semester has finished. Which approach fits best, and why?
choices: Batch, because there is no need for low latency, and batch processes large volumes efficiently over complete data without an always-on system.
Streaming, because it is the modern approach and always gives better results.
Streaming with a 30-second window, so each grade is checked against recent grades as it is entered.
Either approach works equally well, because batch and streaming have the same cost and latency.
questions.why: When results are only needed after all the data exists, batch gives complete, accurate totals cheaply, while streaming would add always-on cost and complexity for no benefit.

questions.prompt: A factory checks for overheating machines by running a batch job every night at 03:00 that reviews the previous day's temperature readings. A motor starts overheating at 10:00 one morning. What is the most likely consequence for the running factory?
choices: The overheating is caught within seconds, because batch jobs check every reading as it arrives.
The overheating is caught immediately, because a batch job uses a window covering the last five minutes.
The batch job cannot process the readings at all, because batch systems only work with financial data.
The overheating is not found until the next night's run, many hours after it began, so damage may already be done.
questions.why: Batch has high latency because it waits for its schedule, so a problem that needs an immediate response is discovered hours late; a streaming design would catch it within seconds.

lessons.explainPrompt: In your own words, explain to a teammate the difference between batch and streaming data processing, and describe one limit or tradeoff of each that should guide which one they choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: Batch processing gathers data over a period and processes it all together in a scheduled run, for example a nightly job that totals the day's sales. Streaming processes each event, such as a payment or sensor reading, within seconds of it arriving. It often uses short time windows to keep running results. The main tradeoff is latency. Batch results arrive late, sometimes hours after the events, so batch is wrong for something like fraud alerts. In return, batch is efficient for large volumes and can calculate over complete data. Streaming gives near-instant answers, but it runs all the time, costs more, is harder to build, and each calculation only sees recent data. I'd pick streaming when someone must act right away. I'd pick batch for reports where waiting is fine, and many systems use both.
rubricPoints: Batch collects data and processes it together on a schedule or once enough has built up.
Streaming processes each event shortly after it arrives, often using time windows.
The deciding factor is how much latency the use case can tolerate.
Batch is efficient and works on complete data but delivers results late.
Streaming gives fast results but costs more, runs continuously and sees only recent data.
A realistic example of each, such as nightly reports versus instant fraud alerts.

suggested.rationale: The unit asks learners to classify scenarios as batch or streaming, so reasoning through exam-style situations after reading the explanation builds that judgement best.

lessons.plain: Real-time analytics means looking at data while it is still arriving, not hours later. Think of a smoke alarm: it reacts within seconds, unlike a weekly inspection report. Microsoft offers several cloud services for this. Azure Event Hubs is a front door that takes in huge numbers of small messages. Azure Stream Analytics reads that flow and runs queries on it continuously. Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence is an all-in-one area for capturing, storing and querying live data and showing it on dashboards. Azure Data Explorer is a fast store for searching large volumes of log and sensor data.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has 500 delivery trucks that each report their location every five seconds, and managers want an alert within a minute when a truck stops unexpectedly. Would you collect the data into files and analyze them once a night, or process it as it arrives? Why?
lessons.teach:
Real-time analytics is the continuous processing of a stream: an unending flow of events. An event is one small record, such as a truck reporting its location and the time. Azure offers distinct services for each job.

Ingestion takes events in. Azure Event Hubs is a managed event-ingestion service, a highly scalable buffer that accepts millions of events per second and holds them briefly for readers. It does not analyze anything itself.

Stream processing analyzes events in motion. Azure Stream Analytics is a managed stream-processing engine. You write a SQL-like query that runs nonstop over incoming events. A window is a time slice the query groups events into. A tumbling window is a run of fixed, non-overlapping slices, for example one per minute. Results go to an output: a database, storage, or a live Power BI dashboard.

Real-time storage and querying keep recent and historical events searchable. Azure Data Explorer is a fast analytics store for large volumes of time-stamped data such as logs and telemetry (sensor readings). It is queried with KQL (Kusto Query Language). Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence bundles these ideas into Fabric's single platform. An eventstream captures and routes live data without code. An eventhouse holds KQL databases for querying. Real-time dashboards show results, and an alerting feature can trigger actions.

Here is a worked example. First, each truck sends an event to Event Hubs. Second, a Stream Analytics query reads those events and averages speed per truck in one-minute tumbling windows. Third, when a truck's average is zero for two windows, the query writes a row to an alert output. Fourth, a Power BI dashboard updates within seconds.

A common mistake is thinking Event Hubs analyzes data. It only ingests. Another mistake is picking a scheduled batch pipeline for a seconds-level need. In a running system, the alert then arrives hours late, after the stalled truck has already missed its deliveries.

questions.prompt:
A wind-energy company wants to spot failing turbines within seconds. Each of its 300 turbines reports a vibration reading every two seconds. Here is the design, with one step missing.

Step 1: Each turbine sends its vibration reading as an event to Azure Event Hubs, the managed event-ingestion service.
Step 2: [missing]
Step 3: When a turbine's maximum vibration is above the safe limit in a five-minute slice, a row is written to an alert output.
Step 4: A live Power BI dashboard shows the flagged turbines within seconds.

Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: A scheduled batch pipeline runs each night and calculates five-minute maximum vibration for every turbine.
A Stream Analytics query reads the events nonstop and finds each turbine's maximum vibration in five-minute tumbling windows.
Event Hubs calculates each turbine's maximum vibration every five minutes before passing results on.
The Power BI dashboard reads raw events from Event Hubs and decides which turbines to flag.
questions.why: Event Hubs only ingests events, so a continuously running Stream Analytics query is what must group readings into fixed five-minute tumbling windows and compute each turbine's maximum before alerting.

questions.prompt: A payment processor runs a Stream Analytics query that counts card transactions in 10-minute tumbling windows starting on the hour. One transaction arrives at 14:03 and another at 14:12. How are they grouped?
choices: Each is counted in two windows, because tumbling windows overlap with their neighbours.
Neither is counted until a scheduled batch job closes the hour.
The 14:03 one falls in the 14:00 to 14:10 slice and the 14:12 one in the 14:10 to 14:20 slice, with no overlap.
Both are counted in one window, because a tumbling window keeps growing until the query stops.
questions.why: A tumbling window is a run of fixed, non-overlapping time slices, so each event belongs to exactly one 10-minute slice.

questions.prompt: An online game studio collects billions of time-stamped server log lines and wants to keep months of them searchable, running fast queries written in KQL (Kusto Query Language). Which Azure service fits this real-time storage and querying need?
choices: Azure Data Explorer
Azure Stream Analytics
A Power BI dashboard
Azure Event Hubs
questions.why: Azure Data Explorer is the fast analytics store for large volumes of time-stamped data such as logs, and it is queried with KQL.

questions.prompt: A hospital needs a warning within seconds when a patient's heart-rate monitor shows a dangerous reading. The team instead builds a scheduled batch pipeline that runs every six hours. What is the most likely consequence once the system is running?
choices: Warnings can arrive hours after the dangerous reading, too late for staff to act in time.
Nothing changes, because a batch pipeline and a stream-processing engine respond equally fast.
Event Hubs will refuse the monitor readings, because it only accepts batch data.
The Power BI dashboard will automatically switch the pipeline to streaming.
questions.why: Choosing a scheduled batch pipeline for a seconds-level need means results only appear when the next run happens, so alerts arrive hours late.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate which Azure services you would combine to show live sensor readings on a dashboard and raise alerts within seconds, what each one does, and one limit or tradeoff of going real-time instead of batch.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd split the job into ingest, process, and present. Azure Event Hubs ingests the sensor events. It's a scalable buffer that just receives them and doesn't analyze them. Azure Stream Analytics then runs a continuous SQL-like query, for example averaging readings over one-minute tumbling windows and flagging anything out of range. It sends results to a live Power BI dashboard and to an alert output. If we also need to search lots of historical telemetry quickly, Azure Data Explorer or a Fabric eventhouse holds it and we query it with KQL. Inside Fabric, Real-Time Intelligence covers the same chain: an eventstream to capture, an eventhouse to store, and real-time dashboards. The tradeoff is that streaming always runs and costs money nonstop. It only sees data within its windows, so heavy reprocessing of years of history is usually cheaper and simpler as a batch job.
rubricPoints: Names Event Hubs as ingestion only, not analysis.
Names Stream Analytics as continuous query processing over windows.
Mentions Fabric Real-Time Intelligence or Azure Data Explorer for storing and querying live data with KQL.
Connects results to a live Power BI or real-time dashboard or an alert.
States a tradeoff, such as constant running cost or a poor fit for large historical reprocessing.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests matching a live-data scenario to the right ingest, process and store service, so reasoning through scenario questions builds that skill best.

lessons.plain: Power BI is Microsoft's tool for turning data into interactive charts, reports and dashboards that people can explore and share. It is a business intelligence tool, meaning software that helps people understand what their data says so they can make decisions. Think of it as the shop window at the end of an analytics pipeline: other services collect, clean and store the goods, and Power BI arranges them so a manager can walk past, see what matters at a glance, and click into any item for more detail. It connects to many data sources, refreshes the view as data changes, and works on desktops, browsers and phones.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sales manager wants one screen showing today's key numbers from several different reports, which she checks on her phone each morning. Do you think she needs a full multi-page report or something simpler, and why?
lessons.teach:
Power BI is a family of business intelligence tools, meaning software that lets people connect to data, shape it, and present it visually so they can make decisions. It sits at the end of an analytics workload: other services ingest and store the data, and Power BI presents it.

It has three main parts. Power BI Desktop is a free application installed on a computer, used to author content. Power BI service is the cloud website where finished content is published, shared, and kept up to date. Power BI mobile apps let people view that content on phones and tablets.

A typical workflow traces like this. First, an author in Desktop connects to sources such as a spreadsheet, a relational database, or an analytical data store. Second, they clean and reshape the data with Power Query, the built-in transformation tool, for example removing blank rows or renaming columns. Third, they relate tables into a data model, a structure that defines how tables link. Fourth, they build a report: one or more pages of interactive visuals, where clicking a bar in one chart filters the others. Fifth, they publish to the service. Sixth, in the service, they pin chosen visuals from one or more reports onto a dashboard, a single-page summary of tiles. Seventh, they schedule refresh, an automatic re-pull of data, and share with colleagues.

Worked example: a retailer's analyst connects Desktop to a sales database, removes test orders in Power Query, builds a three-page report on sales by region, product and month, publishes it, pins the total-revenue and top-region charts to a dashboard, and sets a nightly refresh. The manager opens that dashboard on her phone and taps a tile to drill into the full report.

A common mistake is treating reports and dashboards as the same thing. Reports are multi-page, detailed and built in Desktop or the service; dashboards are single-page, service-only, and gather tiles from several reports. Another mistake is forgetting refresh: without it, published content quietly shows stale numbers and people make decisions on old data.

questions.prompt: A regional bus company's analyst is building Power BI content for the operations director. Step 1: in Power BI Desktop (the free authoring application), she connects to a ridership spreadsheet and a maintenance database. Step 2: in Power Query (the built-in cleaning tool), she removes duplicate trip records. Step 3: she links the tables by bus ID in the data model. Step 4: she builds two multi-page reports, 'Ridership' and 'Fleet Health', and publishes both to the Power BI service (the cloud website). Step 5: the director wants ONE page showing just the on-time-rate chart from Ridership and the breakdowns-per-week chart from Fleet Health. Step 6: she sets a nightly refresh and shares the result. What should Step 5 be?
choices: Use Power Query to merge the two reports into a single page
Open the mobile app and assemble the summary page there
In Desktop, add a fifth page to Ridership and copy the fleet chart onto it
In the service, pin both charts onto a new dashboard
questions.why: A dashboard is a single-page, service-only summary that can gather pinned visuals from several reports, which is exactly what the director asked for.

questions.prompt: In Power BI, which description fits a dashboard rather than a report?
choices: A structure that defines how tables link to each other
A set of Power Query steps that clean data before modeling
Several pages of interactive visuals authored in Power BI Desktop
One page of tiles in the service, pinned from one or more reports
questions.why: Dashboards are single-page, exist only in the Power BI service, and collect tiles pinned from one or more reports; multi-page interactive content is a report.

questions.prompt: A field coordinator at a wildlife charity needs to check already-published donation charts while visiting sites, using only her phone. She does not need to create or edit anything. Which part of Power BI fits her need?
choices: The data model
Power BI mobile apps
Power Query
Power BI Desktop
questions.why: The mobile apps let people view published content on phones and tablets, while Desktop, Power Query and the data model are for authoring and shaping data.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic published a Power BI report on missed appointments in March and never set a scheduled refresh. In June, staff notice the numbers have not changed even though missed appointments clearly rose. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Without scheduled refresh, the published report still shows March data
Only dashboards need refresh, so the report should have updated itself
Power Query automatically deletes any rows added after publishing
The report must be reopened in the mobile app to pull new data
questions.why: Refresh is the automatic re-pull of data; without it, published content quietly keeps showing stale numbers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Power BI does in an analytics solution, walking through how content moves from Desktop to the service and phone, and name one limit or tradeoff, such as the difference between reports and dashboards or the need for refresh.
lessons.modelAnswer: Power BI is the presentation layer of an analytics solution. It does not replace the systems that ingest and store data; it connects to them and turns the data into interactive visuals. An author uses Power BI Desktop to connect to sources, clean the data with Power Query, relate tables into a model, and build a report, which can have several interactive pages. They publish it to the Power BI service in the cloud, where they can pin key visuals from one or more reports onto a dashboard, a single-page overview, and share it so people can view it in a browser or the mobile app. One tradeoff is that a dashboard is quick to read but shallow, so users click through to the report for detail. A limit to watch is refresh: if scheduled refresh is not set up, the published numbers go stale.
rubricPoints: Power BI presents and explores data; it sits at the end of the pipeline rather than storing large-scale data.
Desktop is for authoring, the service is for publishing and sharing, and mobile apps are for viewing.
Power Query is used to clean and reshape data before building visuals.
Reports are multi-page and interactive; dashboards are single-page collections of pinned tiles in the service.
Scheduled refresh keeps published content current, and without it data goes stale.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly a product catalogue of Power BI's parts and workflow, and no listed mission or planned engine exercises Power BI, so careful reading is the best fit.

lessons.plain: A Power BI data model is the organised set of tables behind a report, plus the rules that tie them together and the calculations built on top. Think of a well-run shop's records: one ledger lists every sale, while separate cards describe each product, each customer and each day of the calendar. The model links the ledger to the cards, so when you ask 'how much did we sell of bikes in March?' Power BI knows which sales belong to bikes and to March. It also lets you group items into levels, such as year, then month, then day, so people can drill down from the big picture to the detail.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have one table listing every sale (date, product ID, amount) and another table listing each product (product ID, name, category). How do you think a report tool could show total sales per category, when the category isn't in the sales table at all?
lessons.teach:
A Power BI data model is a collection of tables, the relationships between them, and calculations stored for reporting. A table is a grid of rows and columns loaded from a source. A relationship links a column in one table to a matching column in another, usually a key such as ProductID. Its cardinality says how many rows match on each side; the common case is one-to-many, where one product row matches many sales rows. Filters flow across a relationship, normally from the 'one' side to the 'many' side.

Models are usually arranged as a star schema. A fact table holds measurable events, such as sales amounts. Dimension tables hold descriptive attributes used to slice those facts, such as product, customer or date. The fact table sits in the middle, linked to each dimension.

On top of the tables you add calculations. A measure is a formula, written in a language called DAX, that is evaluated at the moment a visual asks for it, such as Total Sales = sum of Amount. A calculated column is computed row by row when data loads and stored in the table. A hierarchy stacks related columns into levels, such as Year, Quarter, Month, letting users drill down. A dedicated date table enables time comparisons such as year-to-date.

Worked example: Sales has ProductID and Amount; Product has ProductID and Category. You create a one-to-many relationship on ProductID. A chart puts Category on its axis and Total Sales as its value. For the 'Bikes' bar, Power BI filters Product to bike rows, the filter flows through ProductID to Sales, and the measure sums only those sales.

A common mistake is forgetting the relationship. Without it the filter cannot travel, so every category bar shows the same grand total. In a live report that means decision-makers see confident-looking but wrong numbers, so checking relationships is the first step when totals repeat.

questions.prompt: A city library builds a Power BI model. The Loans table has MemberID and BooksBorrowed. The Members table has MemberID and Branch. A one-to-many relationship links Members (one side) to Loans (many side) on MemberID. A bar chart puts Branch on its axis and a measure, Total Books = sum of BooksBorrowed, as its value. Here is how Power BI works out the 'Riverside' bar. Step 1: Power BI filters the Members table to only the rows where Branch is Riverside. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: The Total Books measure is evaluated and adds up BooksBorrowed only for the rows that are left. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: The filter flows from Loans up to Members, so Members keeps only rows with loans.
A calculated column in Loans is recomputed for Riverside when the chart is drawn.
The measure adds every loan in the library, then splits the total evenly by branch.
The filter flows through MemberID into Loans, keeping only Riverside members' loans.
questions.why: Filters normally travel across a relationship from the 'one' side (Members) to the 'many' side (Loans) through the shared key, so only Riverside members' loan rows remain for the measure to sum.

questions.prompt: A hospital analyst wants a value called Average Wait Minutes. It must recalculate whenever a report user slices by ward, by month or by doctor, rather than being fixed when the data loads. In a Power BI data model, which feature should hold this calculation?
choices: A one-to-many relationship on WardID
A calculated column added to the visits table
A hierarchy of Ward, Month and Doctor
A measure written in DAX
questions.why: A measure is a DAX formula that is evaluated when a visual asks for it, so it responds to whatever filters are applied. A calculated column is computed row by row at load time and stored.

questions.prompt: A gym chain loads three tables into Power BI. Visits has VisitDate, MemberID, ClubID and MinutesSpent. Member has MemberID, Name and MembershipPlan. Club has ClubID, Town and Manager. The model is arranged as a star schema. Which table is the fact table?
choices: Club, because it is the table that every other table links to
Member, because every visit depends on a member existing
Visits, because it records measurable events such as minutes spent
None of them, because a star schema needs a dedicated date table first
questions.why: The fact table holds measurable events, here each visit and its minutes, and sits in the middle of the star. Member and Club hold descriptive attributes, so they are dimension tables.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain's Power BI report shows a bar chart with Store on the axis and Total Revenue as the value. Every store's bar shows exactly 48,200, which is the revenue for the whole chain. What is the most likely cause, and the first thing to check?
choices: The Store column has not been placed into a hierarchy, so drill-down is disabled
No relationship links the Store table to the Sales table, so the filter cannot travel
The relationship between Store and Sales is one-to-many instead of many-to-many
The model has no date table, so time comparisons are blocking the store filter
questions.why: When every category shows the same grand total, the store filter is not reaching the sales rows, which usually means the relationship is missing; one-to-many is the normal, correct cardinality here.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Power BI data model lets a report show sales by product category, naming the parts involved, and describe one limit or tradeoff, such as when to use a measure versus a calculated column.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Power BI data model is the set of tables, relationships and calculations a report sits on. We usually build a star schema: a fact table like Sales with the amounts, surrounded by dimension tables like Product and Date that describe them. A one-to-many relationship on ProductID links each product to its many sales, and filters flow from Product to Sales. So when a chart groups by Category, the category filter reaches the sales rows and a measure, a DAX formula like sum of Amount, adds up just those. Hierarchies such as Year to Month let users drill down. The tradeoff: a calculated column is computed once per row at load time and stored, so it takes memory but can be used to slice; a measure is computed on demand for whatever filters apply, so it's flexible for totals. And if a relationship is missing, every group shows the same grand total.
rubricPoints: Defines the model as tables plus relationships plus calculations.
Describes a star schema with a fact table and dimension tables.
Explains that a one-to-many relationship on a key lets filters flow from dimension to fact.
Distinguishes measures (computed on demand) from calculated columns (stored per row).
Mentions hierarchies or a date table for drill-down and time analysis.
Names a limit, such as missing relationships causing repeated totals or calculated columns costing memory.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine builds Power BI models, and explaining how tables, relationships and measures combine to answer a scenario is the core skill the exam tests.

lessons.plain: Choosing a visualization means picking the kind of picture that best answers the question someone is asking of the data. A chart is a tool, and like any tool each type suits a particular job. You would not use a hammer to cut a board, and you would not use a pie chart to show how sales rose month by month. In Power BI, Microsoft's reporting tool, you build reports from visuals, which are charts, tables, maps and single numbers. The skill is matching the question, such as comparing, spotting a trend, showing a share, finding a relationship or locating something, to the visual that makes the answer obvious at a glance.
lessons.guessPrompt: A manager wants to see whether website visits went up or down over the last twelve months. Which kind of chart would you reach for first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A visualization, often shortened to visual, is a graphical display of data on a report page. In Power BI, a report is a set of pages holding visuals that all draw on the same data model, which is the organized set of tables behind the report. The right visual depends on the question being asked.

To compare amounts across categories, such as sales per region, use a bar chart (horizontal bars) or a column chart (vertical bars). Lengths are easy for the eye to compare. To show a trend over time, use a line chart, because the connected line shows direction and rate of change. To show parts of a whole, use a pie or donut chart for a few slices, or a treemap, which is nested rectangles sized by value and works when there are many items or a hierarchy. To show the relationship between two numeric measures, use a scatter chart, where each dot is one item placed by two values. For location data, use a map. For a single headline figure, use a card, which shows one large number. A KPI visual shows a key performance indicator, meaning a measure judged against a target. A table lists rows and columns of detail, and a matrix is a table that can group and subtotal rows and columns like a pivot table. A slicer is an on-page filter control that lets viewers narrow what every other visual shows.

Worked example: a retailer asks three questions. First, which store sells most? That is a comparison across categories, so use a column chart of sales by store. Second, are monthly sales growing? That is a trend over time, so use a line chart with months on the horizontal axis. Third, does advertising spend relate to sales? That is two numeric measures, so use a scatter chart with one dot per store. A slicer for year lets viewers filter all three at once.

A common mistake is a pie chart with fifteen slices. Thin slices are hard to compare, so readers misjudge which is bigger. In a live report that leads to wrong decisions, so switch to a bar chart once categories go beyond a handful.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency is building a Power BI report and needs one visual for each of three questions. Question 1: which of its 8 bus routes carried the most riders last month? That compares amounts across categories, so the analyst uses a bar chart of riders by route. Question 2: what share of riders paid with each of the 3 fare types (cash, card, monthly pass)? That is parts of a whole with only a few slices, so the analyst uses a donut chart. Question 3: has daily ridership been rising or falling over the past 12 months? Which visual should the analyst choose for Question 3, and why?
choices: A line chart with dates on the horizontal axis, because the connected line shows the direction and rate of change
A treemap, because twelve months is too many items for a pie chart
A card, because ridership is a single number viewers want to see
A scatter chart, because each day becomes a dot placed by two values
questions.why: Question 3 asks about a trend over time, and a line chart's connected line shows whether values go up or down and how fast.

questions.prompt: A finance analyst wants a visual that lists expense rows by department and by quarter, groups them, and shows subtotals for each department and each quarter, much like a pivot table. Which Power BI visual fits?
choices: Table
Matrix
Slicer
Card
questions.why: A matrix is a table that can group and subtotal rows and columns like a pivot table, while a plain table only lists rows and columns of detail.

questions.prompt: A charity wants the top of its dashboard to show this quarter's total donations, 41,000, judged against its quarterly goal of 50,000, so viewers can see at a glance how it is doing against target. Which visual fits best?
choices: A pie chart with two slices: raised and not yet raised
A card, because it shows one large number
A KPI visual, because it shows a measure judged against a target
A scatter chart of donations against the goal
questions.why: A KPI visual is designed to show a key performance indicator, a measure compared with a target, whereas a card only shows the single number with no target.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop's report uses a pie chart to show revenue share across 22 book genres. Managers keep misjudging which genres earn more because many slices are thin. What is the best fix?
choices: Replace it with a line chart of revenue by genre
Replace it with a card showing total revenue
Replace it with a bar chart of revenue by genre
Change it to a donut chart with the same 22 slices
questions.why: Once categories go beyond a handful, thin slices are hard to compare, and a bar chart's lengths are easy to compare across many categories.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide which Power BI visual to use for a given question, and name one situation where a popular chart type becomes a poor choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the question, not the chart. If someone wants to compare amounts across categories, like revenue per product line, I use a bar or column chart because lengths are easy to compare. If they ask how something changed over time, I use a line chart with time on the horizontal axis. For a share of a total, a pie or donut works for a few categories, and a treemap handles many items or a hierarchy. If they ask whether two numbers move together, I use a scatter chart. Locations go on a map, a single headline number goes on a card, a figure measured against a target goes in a KPI visual, and exact detail goes in a table or matrix. Slicers let viewers filter the whole page. The tradeoff: pie charts break down past about five or six slices because thin wedges are hard to compare, so a sorted bar chart is clearer there.
rubricPoints: Starts from the question being asked rather than from a favorite chart.
Matches comparison to bar or column charts and trends over time to line charts.
Matches parts of a whole to pie, donut or treemap, and relationships between two measures to scatter charts.
Mentions cards or KPI visuals for single figures and tables or matrices for detail.
Names a limit, such as pie charts becoming unreadable with many categories.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine builds reports, and the exam tests this by giving a scenario and asking which visual fits, so reasoning through short business scenarios builds the skill best.

scenarios.title: Harbourline Bikes: Sorting Out the Rental Data
scenarios.scenario:
Harbourline Bikes is a fictional company that rents electric bikes from street docks in three cities. You have just joined its small data team, and your manager wants to check that you can describe its data correctly before you touch anything.

Harbourline has three kinds of data. First, a rentals table: every time a customer unlocks a bike, the app writes one row with the same fixed columns (RentalID, CustomerID, BikeID, StartTime, EndTime, Price). A row is one record, and a column is one named field that every row shares. Second, bike telemetry: every minute each bike sends a small JSON message. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format that stores data as named fields and values, for example {"bikeId": 812, "battery": 64, "gps": {"lat": 51.5, "lon": -0.1}}. Newer bikes add extra fields such as "tyrePressure" that older bikes do not send. Third, damage photos: when a customer reports a broken bike, they upload a JPEG image (a common compressed picture file format) taken on their phone.

The company uses this data in two ways. The checkout system records each rental, charges the card, and must never record half a rental or charge a customer twice, even when hundreds of people unlock bikes at the same moment. Separately, once a month the finance director looks at a report showing total revenue and average ride length per city over the past two years.

Three people work with this data. Priya makes sure the rentals database is backed up every night, decides who is allowed to read or change it, and applies security updates. Tom builds the automated process that copies rental rows and telemetry each night into a separate store built for reporting, cleaning out bad readings on the way. Grace takes the cleaned data, explores it, and builds the dashboard the finance director reads.

Answer the following.

1. Classify the rentals table, the bike telemetry, and the damage photos as structured, semi-structured, or unstructured data, and give the reason for each.

2. Classify the checkout system and the monthly finance report as a transactional workload or an analytical workload, and give two features of each that support your answer.

3. Name the data role that Priya, Tom, and Grace each perform (database administrator, data engineer, or data analyst), and explain which of their tasks shows it.

4. Suggest a suitable kind of Azure data store for each of the three kinds of data, naming the Azure service and saying in plain terms what kind of store it is and why it fits.
modelAnswer: The rentals table is structured data: every row has the same fixed set of columns with known data types, so it fits neatly into a table defined by a schema (a schema is the agreed layout of fields and their types, decided before data is stored). The bike telemetry is semi-structured data: each JSON message has named fields, so it carries some organisation, but the fields can vary between messages (newer bikes add tyrePressure, and gps is nested inside another field), so it does not fit one rigid table layout. The damage photos are unstructured data: a JPEG image has no named fields or rows that describe its contents; the information is in the pixels and needs a person or special software to interpret it. A strong answer gives the reason, not just the label.
