The checkout system is a transactional workload, also called OLTP (online transaction processing). Supporting features: it handles many small, fast reads and writes as each rental happens; each rental must be recorded completely or not at all, and data must stay correct when many people act at once (the ACID guarantees: atomicity means all-or-nothing, consistency means rules are never broken, isolation means simultaneous transactions do not interfere, durability means a saved change survives a crash). The monthly report is an analytical workload. Supporting features: it reads large amounts of historical data (two years) rather than writing new records; it summarises data with totals and averages to spot trends and support decisions; it usually runs on a copy of the data held in a store built for reporting, not on the live checkout system. The consequence of mixing them up: running heavy two-year summaries directly on the checkout database could slow down unlocks and payments for customers. Any two valid features per workload earn credit.

Priya is the database administrator (DBA): she runs nightly backups so data can be restored after a failure, controls access by deciding who can read or change the database, and keeps the database secure and up to date. Tom is the data engineer: he builds and runs the automated pipeline (a repeatable process that moves and transforms data) that copies rental and telemetry data into the reporting store and cleans out bad readings on the way. Grace is the data analyst: she explores the cleaned data to find meaning and builds the dashboard (a visual report) that the finance director uses to make decisions. A common mistake is calling Tom an analyst because he works with reporting data; his job is moving and preparing data, not interpreting it.

Rentals table: Azure SQL Database, a managed relational database (the cloud provider runs the server, patching, and backups infrastructure, while data is stored in tables with fixed columns that can be linked by keys). It fits because the data is structured and the checkout system needs reliable transactions. Bike telemetry: Azure Cosmos DB, a managed non-relational (NoSQL) database that stores JSON documents without requiring every document to have the same fields, so it fits semi-structured messages whose fields vary and arrive in large numbers. Damage photos: Azure Blob Storage, a cloud object store for large files of any type (a blob is a binary large object, simply a file stored as-is), which fits unstructured images that do not belong in table rows. Storing the telemetry as files in Azure Data Lake Storage, or using Azure Database for PostgreSQL or MySQL for rentals, are also acceptable if justified with the same reasoning.

scenarios.title: Moving Harbor Lane Bakeries off spreadsheets and onto Azure
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lane Bakeries is a fictional chain of six bakeries. For years, all customer orders have lived in one big spreadsheet. Every row holds an order number, the order date, the customer's name, the customer's email, the customer's phone number, the product name, and the product price. A regular customer who has ordered 40 times has their name, email and phone typed out 40 separate times. Last month a customer changed her email, staff updated only some of her rows, and confirmation emails went to the wrong address.

You have just joined the small engineering team. Your lead wants to move this data into a relational database, which is a database that stores data in tables (grids of rows and columns), where each table describes one kind of thing and tables are linked to each other through shared values called keys. A primary key is a column whose value uniquely identifies each row in its table, such as a customer number. A foreign key is a column in one table that holds the primary key of a row in another table, which is how the two tables are linked.

Your lead also mentions three other systems that need a home in Azure, Microsoft's cloud platform. First, the company's existing order-tracking application runs on Microsoft SQL Server (Microsoft's relational database software) in the back office. It relies on SQL Server Agent, a built-in scheduler that runs jobs such as nightly clean-ups, and on queries that read from two databases on the same server at once. The team wants to move it to the cloud with as few code changes as possible and does not want to patch operating systems. Second, a supplier-ordering tool bought from a vendor needs a specific third-party program installed directly on the same machine as SQL Server, and the vendor requires administrator access to the operating system. Third, a new loyalty-points website was built by a contractor on PostgreSQL, a popular open-source relational database (open-source meaning its source code is freely available and not owned by one vendor), and the team wants Azure to handle backups and patching for it.

Answer the following.

1. Explain what normalization is, why the current spreadsheet causes the email problem, and propose how to split the spreadsheet data into tables, naming the primary key and any foreign keys for each table.

2. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for working with relational databases. Name the SQL statement you would use for each of these tasks and say whether it belongs to the group that defines the structure of the database (Data Definition Language, DDL) or the group that works with the data inside it (Data Manipulation Language, DML): (a) building the new Customers table, (b) fixing the customer's email address, (c) listing all orders placed in June.

3. The bakery managers want to see a simple list of order number, date, customer name and product name without needing to understand how the tables are joined. They should not be able to see customer phone numbers. Name the database object you would create and explain how it meets both needs.

4. Choose the best Azure service for each of the three other systems (the order-tracking application, the supplier-ordering tool, and the loyalty-points website) and give a one- or two-sentence reason for each.
subParts: Choose SQL statements and their type
Pick a database object for managers
Match each system to an Azure service
modelAnswer: Normalization is the process of organizing data into separate, related tables so that each fact is stored in only one place. It reduces duplicated data and prevents update errors. The spreadsheet repeats the customer's email on every order row, so changing it means editing many rows; if any are missed, the data contradicts itself, which is exactly what sent emails to the wrong address. A good split: a Customers table (CustomerID as primary key, plus Name, Email, Phone); a Products table (ProductID as primary key, plus ProductName, Price); an Orders table (OrderID as primary key, OrderDate, and CustomerID as a foreign key pointing to Customers). Because one order can contain several products, a strong answer adds an OrderItems (order lines) table with OrderID and ProductID as foreign keys, plus Quantity, where the pair of OrderID and ProductID (or a separate line ID) acts as the primary key. Now the email lives in one row of Customers, so one change fixes it everywhere. Award full credit if the learner defines normalization, links the duplication to the update error, and gives at least Customers, Products and Orders with correct primary and foreign keys; the order-lines table is a bonus, not required.

(a) CREATE TABLE, which is DDL because it defines the structure of the database. (b) UPDATE, which is DML because it changes existing data, for example UPDATE Customers SET Email = the new address WHERE CustomerID = her ID. A strong answer warns that leaving out the WHERE clause would change every customer's email. (c) SELECT, which is DML in this course's grouping because it works with the data (some sources list it separately as a query statement, which is also acceptable), with a WHERE condition limiting OrderDate to June. Full credit needs the correct statement and the correct group for all three.

Create a view. A view is a saved query that behaves like a virtual table: it stores no data of its own and shows results drawn from the real tables each time it is used. The view would join Orders, Customers, Products (and order lines if present) and return only order number, order date, customer name and product name. Managers query the view as if it were one simple table, so they do not need to know how the joins work. Because the phone column is simply left out of the view and managers are given permission to the view rather than the underlying tables, they cannot see phone numbers. Full credit needs the term view, the idea that it is a saved query or virtual table, and an explanation of both the simplification and the hiding of columns.

Order-tracking application: Azure SQL Managed Instance, a managed cloud version of SQL Server where Microsoft handles the operating system and patching, and which offers near-complete compatibility with on-premises SQL Server, including SQL Server Agent and queries across databases on the same instance, so the app moves with few code changes. Azure SQL Database is not the best fit because it is a single managed database without SQL Server Agent or easy cross-database queries. Supplier-ordering tool: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, meaning SQL Server installed on a cloud virtual machine (a software-based computer you rent). It is the only option of the three that gives full administrator control of the operating system so the third-party program can be installed alongside SQL Server; the trade-off is that the team must patch and maintain the machine themselves. Loyalty-points website: Azure Database for PostgreSQL, a managed service that runs open-source PostgreSQL with backups, patching and high availability handled by Azure, so the contractor's code works unchanged. Full credit needs the correct service and a reason tied to the stated requirement for each of the three.

scenarios.title: Harbourlight Outfitters Moves Its Non-Relational Data to Azure
scenarios.scenario:
Harbourlight Outfitters is a fictional outdoor-gear retailer with an office, a warehouse, and an online shop that sells to customers in Europe, North America, and Asia. You have joined the data team. Your lead wants every workload matched to a specific Azure feature, not just a general answer like 'put it in the cloud'.

Some terms first. Non-relational data is data that is not stored in fixed tables of rows and columns linked by relationships. Examples include images, files, and flexible records. Azure Storage is Microsoft's general cloud storage service. Within it, Azure Blob storage holds unstructured objects called blobs (binary large objects), such as images or videos. Azure Files offers shared folders in the cloud. Azure Table storage keeps simple key-value records, where each record is found by its keys. Azure Cosmos DB is a fully managed, globally distributable NoSQL database, meaning a database that is not built around fixed relational tables. An API (application programming interface) is the set of commands an application uses to talk to a service. Cosmos DB offers several APIs so that apps written for other databases can use it.

Here is what the team needs.

The marketing team has about 4 TB of product photos and short videos. New images are viewed constantly on the website. Images older than a year are almost never opened, but they must be kept for seven years for legal reasons, and a retrieval delay of several hours is acceptable for them.

The office still uses an old Windows file server. Staff open a mapped network drive (a shared folder that shows up like a drive letter, for example H:) using the SMB protocol, which stands for Server Message Block, the standard Windows file-sharing method. The server is failing, and staff want to keep using a mapped drive without changing how they work.

The warehouse has 300 handheld barcode scanners. Each scanner sends small status records: scanner ID, time, battery level, and last location. The records are always looked up by scanner ID and time. No joins or complex queries are needed, and the budget is very tight.

The online shop's shopping-cart and product-catalog service was written for MongoDB, a popular document database that stores records as JSON documents. JSON is a text format of named fields. Customers in Asia complain the shop is slow, because the database runs in a single European data centre. The developers do not want to rewrite their database code.

Your tasks:
1. Name the Azure service and the specific feature that fits the marketing images and videos, including how to handle the older files cheaply.
2. Name the Azure service and feature that replaces the failing office file server.
3. Name the Azure service that fits the scanner status records, and explain how each record would be identified.
4. Name the Azure service and the specific API for the shopping-cart and catalog service, and the feature that fixes slow access for customers in Asia.
modelAnswer: Use Azure Blob storage, which stores unstructured objects such as images and video. Store them as block blobs, the blob type designed for files that are uploaded and then read. Use access tiers, which are price levels that trade storage cost against access cost and speed. Keep current images in the Hot tier, which costs more to store but is cheap and fast to read. Move images older than a year to the Archive tier, which is the cheapest to store but is offline: a file must be rehydrated (brought back online), which can take hours. That delay is acceptable here. The Cool tier is a middle option for data read occasionally. A lifecycle management policy, a rule that moves blobs between tiers automatically by age, can do the moving. A common mistake is to leave everything in Hot. Archive is not the wrong choice; it simply has a retrieval delay that is fine for these files.

Use Azure Files to create a cloud file share. A file share is a shared folder that many users or machines can open at the same time. Azure Files supports the SMB protocol, so office PCs can map the share as a network drive, such as H:, just as they did with the old server. Staff keep the same way of working, and the failing hardware is retired. A common mistake is to choose Blob storage. Blob storage is reached through web-style requests by applications. It is not a mapped drive that staff browse with SMB, so it would change how staff work.

Use Azure Table storage. It is a low-cost key-value store for large numbers of simple, structured records with no fixed schema and no joins. Each record, called an entity, is identified by two keys. The partition key groups related entities; here it would be the scanner ID. The row key uniquely identifies an entity within its partition; here it would be the timestamp. Together, the partition key and row key form the unique identifier, and lookups by them are fast. This fits because the records are small, always looked up by scanner and time, and the budget is tight. A common mistake is to choose a relational database, which adds cost and structure the workload does not need.

Use Azure Cosmos DB with the API for MongoDB. This API lets an application written for MongoDB talk to Cosmos DB using its existing MongoDB code and drivers, so developers do not need a rewrite. To fix the slow access in Asia, use global distribution: add Azure regions in Asia and North America so Cosmos DB replicates (copies) the data there. Customers then read from a nearby copy, which lowers latency, meaning the delay before a response arrives. Multi-region writes can also be enabled so carts are updated close to the customer. A common mistake is to pick the default NoSQL API, which would force a code rewrite. Another is to keep a single region, which leaves the latency problem in place.

scenarios.title: Brightmoor Bikes: Live Dock Status and Nightly Ride Reports
scenarios.scenario:
Brightmoor Bikes is a fictional bike-sharing company with 400 docking stations across one city. You have just joined its small data team, and your manager wants a plan for its first analytics workload. An analytics workload is the set of steps that collect data, store it in a form suited to analysis, and present it so people can make decisions.

The company has two kinds of data. First, every dock has a sensor. A sensor is a small device that reports a reading. Each one sends a short message every few seconds saying how many bikes are parked and whether the dock is working. Each message is called an event. Operations staff want a screen showing which stations are empty or full right now, so a van can move bikes before customers complain. Second, every night at 1 a.m. the payment system exports a file. To export is to copy data out of one system so another can use it. The file lists every ride completed that day: ride ID, start station, end station, start time, duration, and price paid. Finance wants reports on revenue and ride trends by month, station, and day of the week.

Some terms you will need. Ingestion means bringing data from where it is created into the place where it will be analysed. Batch processing means collecting data over a period and handling it together on a schedule, such as once a night. Streaming processing means handling each event within seconds of its arrival, without waiting for a group to build up. A data lake is cheap storage that holds large amounts of raw files in any format. A data warehouse is a store that holds cleaned, structured tables built for fast reporting queries. A lakehouse combines the two: files sit in a data lake, and a table layer on top lets you query them like a warehouse. Microsoft Fabric is a Microsoft cloud service that brings these pieces together in one product: ingestion, lakehouse and warehouse storage, real-time analytics, and Power BI reporting. Azure Databricks is a Microsoft cloud service for large-scale data processing. It runs Apache Spark, an open-source engine that splits big jobs across many computers working in parallel. Azure Stream Analytics is a managed service that reads a live stream of events and runs continuous queries over it. Managed means Microsoft runs the servers for you. Real-Time Intelligence is the part of Microsoft Fabric that captures, stores, and queries streaming events. Power BI is Microsoft's tool for building interactive reports and dashboards. A report is a set of pages of charts you can click to filter. A dashboard is a single page of key tiles for quick checking. Every report in Power BI sits on a data model. A data model is the set of tables a report reads from, the relationships that link them, and the calculations defined on them.

Your manager asks you to answer the following.

1. For each of the two data flows, the dock sensor events and the nightly ride file, say whether it should be handled as batch or streaming, and give the reason.
2. Name a Microsoft cloud service that could process the dock sensor events so the operations screen stays current, and describe in generic terms what that service does.
3. Recommend where the nightly ride data should be stored for finance reporting, and name a Microsoft service that could hold it. Say when Azure Databricks would be a sensible addition.
4. Describe how the Power BI data model for the ride reports should be arranged. Then pick a suitable visual for each of these: monthly revenue over the past two years, total rides today as a single headline number, and ride counts per station shown by location.
subParts: Batch or streaming for each flow
Power BI model and visual choices
modelAnswer:
The dock sensor events should be streaming. The operations team needs to know which stations are empty or full right now. Each event is only useful if it is handled within seconds of arriving. Collecting the events and processing them once a night would show yesterday's picture, and vans would be sent to the wrong stations.

The nightly ride file should be batch. It already arrives as one complete file on a schedule, and finance looks at trends over months. A delay of a few hours does no harm, and processing the whole file in one scheduled run is simpler and cheaper.

A common mistake is to assume streaming is always better. Streaming costs more and adds complexity, so use it only where the decision really depends on data from the last few seconds.

Azure Stream Analytics would fit. It is a managed stream-processing service: it reads events as they arrive and runs a query that never stops. For example, it could take the latest bike count per dock and flag any station with zero bikes or no free spaces. It then sends those results to an output that the operations screen reads, such as a store or a Power BI dashboard.

Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric is also an acceptable answer. It captures streaming events, stores them, and lets you query them within seconds.

In generic terms, both are a real-time analytics engine. It keeps processing an unending flow of events instead of running once over a finished file.

Load each night's file into a data lake as raw storage. Then clean it into structured tables in a lakehouse or a data warehouse, which is built for fast reporting queries. Finance reports read from those tables.

Microsoft Fabric could hold the data, using its lakehouse or its warehouse. Both are analytical data stores, and Fabric's Power BI can read them directly.

Azure Databricks would be a sensible addition when the data grows very large or needs heavy transformation. In that case, Spark spreads the work across many computers so the nightly job finishes in time. For a single city's daily ride file, it is probably not needed at first.

A common mistake is to run finance reports straight against the live payment system. Heavy report queries could slow down customer payments.

Arrange the model as a star schema, a layout where one central table links out to several lookup tables. The centre is a fact table: one row per ride, holding the numbers to add up, such as price and duration, plus keys that link to other tables. A key is a column whose value matches a row in another table. Around it sit dimension tables, which describe the facts and are used to filter and group them. Here those are a Station table (name and location), and a Date table (day, month, and day of the week). One-to-many relationships connect each dimension to the fact table. One-to-many means one station row matches many ride rows. Define measures, which are reusable calculations, for Total Revenue (the sum of price) and Ride Count (the number of rides). Because of the relationships, one click on a station or month filters every visual on the page.

Visuals: use a line chart for monthly revenue over two years, since it shows a trend over time. Use a card, a visual that shows one large number, for total rides today. Use a map visual for ride counts by station, plotting each station at its location.

A common mistake is a pie chart with 24 monthly slices, which hides the trend.
